title: Random Matrix Spectra from Boltzmann-Weighted Lattice Ensembles
summary: We introduce a random matrix framework for studying statistical-mechanical lattice systems through spectral observables. Equilibrium configurations sampled from a Boltzmann measure are mapped to matrix ensembles whose covariance structure is inherited from the spatial correlations of the underlying model. This construction maps real-space correlation functions to a momentum-space variance profile, providing a direct bridge between statistical-mechanical correlations and correlated random matrix ensembles. We derive this variance profile in finite-correlation-length and critical regimes, and compute spectral moments within a Wick-contraction expansion. A complementary self-consistent description of the bulk density is developed using the resolvent formalism. These analytical methods are benchmarked against Monte Carlo data for the two-dimensional Ising model and three-dimensional Edwards--Anderson spin glasses. In both cases, the spectra evolve from the semicircle law at high temperature to model-dependent critical forms reflecting the structure of correlations. The framework, therefore, provides a quantitative spectral route to probing collective behavior in ordered and disordered statistical systems, while also defining a class of physically motivated correlated random matrix ensembles.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a random matrix framework that maps equilibrium configurations of statistical-mechanical lattice systems to correlated random matrix ensembles, using spectral observables to probe collective behavior. The method bridges spatial correlations to spectral properties, is validated on 2D Ising and 3D Edwards-Anderson spin glass models, and shows spectra transitioning from semicircle law to critical forms.
AI.motivation: To provide a quantitative spectral route for probing collective behavior in statistical-mechanical systems by mapping spatial correlations to spectral observables via random matrix theory.
AI.method: Equilibrium configurations from Boltzmann measures are mapped to matrix ensembles; real-space correlation functions are transformed into a momentum-space variance profile. Spectral moments are computed via Wick-contraction expansion, and the bulk density is described using resolvent formalism. Analytical results are benchmarked against Monte Carlo simulations.
AI.result: Spectra evolve from the semicircle law at high temperature to model-dependent critical forms reflecting correlation structure. Validated on 2D Ising model and 3D Edwards-Anderson spin glasses.
AI.conclusion: The framework defines a class of physically motivated correlated random matrix ensembles and provides a spectral route to studying ordered and disordered statistical systems.

title: Dynamical systems on ultra small-world networks
summary: Despite the knowledge that social, economical, and ecological networks are often of a small-world nature with inter-nodal distance growing even slower than logarithmically with system size, we often assume theoretical systems to be outside of this regime, to make them easier to treat analytically. Here we derive a framework to apply the powerful dynamical mean-field theory on highly heterogeneous networks that is able to account for more of the degree correlations naturally arising from network constraints, known as structural cut-offs. We apply this framework to the well-studied and understood disordered Lotka-Volterra model, and show typically reported observables such as survival rates and stability for these systems on ultra small-world networks. We find much better agreement for these variables for all ranges of exponents for simulated power-law networks as well as empirically sourced networks.

AI.tldr: The paper develops a dynamical mean-field theory framework for highly heterogeneous networks that accounts for degree correlations from structural cut-offs, applies it to the Lotka-Volterra model on ultra small-world networks, and shows improved agreement with simulated and empirical power-law networks for survival rates and stability.
AI.motivation: Real-world social, economic, and ecological networks exhibit ultra small-world properties with inter-nodal distance growing slower than logarithmically with system size, yet theoretical models often assume systems outside this regime for analytical tractability. The authors aim to bridge this gap by developing a framework that can handle the degree correlations arising from network constraints (structural cut-offs) in highly heterogeneous networks.
AI.method: The authors derive a dynamical mean-field theory (DMFT) framework for highly heterogeneous networks that incorporates degree correlations from structural cut-offs. They apply this framework to the disordered Lotka-Volterra model on ultra small-world networks, testing it on simulated power-law networks with various exponent ranges and empirically sourced networks.
AI.result: The proposed framework shows much better agreement for survival rates and stability observables across all ranges of exponents for both simulated power-law networks and empirically sourced networks, compared to typically reported results that assume systems outside the ultra small-world regime.
AI.conclusion: Accounting for structural cut-offs and degree correlations in DMFT significantly improves predictions for ecological dynamics on realistic ultra small-world networks, demonstrating the importance of network constraints in theoretical modeling of complex systems.

title: Temperature-induced optical enhancement near a localization transition
summary: Quasiperiodic systems are an intermediate class of systems between periodic crystals and disordered systems, famously exhibiting metal-insulator transitions (MITs) even in one dimension. While their transport properties have been studied extensively, a systematic analysis of the finite-frequency optical conductivity near the critical point has been lacking. In this work, we carry out a detailed study of the optical conductivity in the paradigmatic Aubry-André model. We find that the zero-temperature low-frequency optical signal is strongly restructured by the quasiperiodic potential, exhibiting an optical gap that closes discontinuously as the system approaches the MIT. Most strikingly, we uncover a mechanism for a strong enhancement of the low-frequency finite temperature optical conductivity at certain resonant frequencies. This enhancement stems from the thermal activation of Pauli-blocked transitions between strongly resonant van Hove singularities. This mechanism provides new insight into finite-frequency transport in quasiperiodic systems and a new pathway for manipulating optical properties near a localization transition. Furthermore, our findings establish the optical response as a powerful, experimentally accessible tool for probing non-trivial quasiperiodicity effects.

AI.tldr: The paper studies the optical conductivity of the Aubry-André model, finding a discontinuous optical gap closing at the metal-insulator transition and a strong enhancement of low-frequency optical conductivity at finite temperatures due to thermal activation of Pauli-blocked transitions between resonant van Hove singularities.
AI.motivation: A systematic analysis of finite-frequency optical conductivity near the critical point of quasiperiodic systems has been lacking, despite extensive study of their transport properties.
AI.method: Detailed study of optical conductivity in the Aubry-André model, a paradigmatic quasiperiodic system.
AI.result: (1) Zero-temperature low-frequency optical signal is strongly restructured, exhibiting an optical gap that closes discontinuously near the MIT. (2) Strong enhancement of low-frequency finite-temperature optical conductivity at resonant frequencies, caused by thermal activation of Pauli-blocked transitions between strongly resonant van Hove singularities.
AI.conclusion: The findings provide new insight into finite-frequency transport in quasiperiodic systems, establish a new pathway for manipulating optical properties near a localization transition, and demonstrate optical response as a powerful experimental tool for probing non-trivial quasiperiodicity effects.

title: Entanglement Growth from Structured Initial States in Many-Body Localized Systems
summary: Understanding how complex entanglement structures emerge is a central problem in quantum many-body physics. Recent work by Zhang et al. has considered structured initial states prepared by evolving a product state under a chaotic Hamiltonian for a finite time before quenching to the target Hamiltonian. In this setup, total entanglement entropy growth in many-body localized systems exhibits two distinct regimes, first increasing and then decreasing as the initial entanglement is tuned. In this work, we identify the physical origin of this behavior by analyzing the dynamics of both the Rényi entanglement entropy and the Wehrl-Rényi entropy in the random-field XXZ model, the latter of which characterizes multipartite entanglement. We show that a similar non-monotonic dependence on the initial entanglement also appears in the net growth of the Wehrl-Rényi entropy for product states polarized along the $z$-direction. The first regime is governed by a finite magnetization associated with local integrals of motion, while the second reflects inter-site correlations. In contrast, for product states in the $x/y$-direction, the entanglement growth exhibits a monotonic decay. Our results provide a more fine-grained picture of how distinct initial-state properties shape entanglement dynamics in many-body localized systems.

AI.tldr: This paper identifies the physical origin of non-monotonic entanglement entropy growth in many-body localized systems by analyzing Rényi and Wehrl-Rényi entropies in the random-field XXZ model, showing that the two regimes are governed by local magnetization and inter-site correlations respectively, with directional dependence for initial product states.
AI.motivation: Understanding how complex entanglement structures emerge is a central problem in quantum many-body physics. The authors aim to identify the physical origin of non-monotonic entanglement growth observed in many-body localized systems when initial states are prepared with varying entanglement.
AI.method: The authors analyze the dynamics of both the Rényi entanglement entropy and the Wehrl-Rényi entropy in the random-field XXZ model, studying product states polarized along different directions ($z$-direction vs. $x/y$-direction).
AI.result: Non-monotonic dependence on initial entanglement also appears in the net growth of Wehrl-Rényi entropy for $z$-polarized product states. The first regime is governed by finite magnetization from local integrals of motion, while the second reflects inter-site correlations. For $x/y$-direction product states, entanglement growth exhibits monotonic decay.
AI.conclusion: The results provide a more fine-grained picture of how distinct initial-state properties shape entanglement dynamics in many-body localized systems.

title: Quantum End-to-End Learning for Contextual Combinatorial Optimization
summary: Contextual combinatorial optimization (CCO) plays a critical role in decision-making under uncertainty, yet remains a significant challenge. We present Quantum End-to-End Learning (QEL), the first quantum computing-based end-to-end learning framework for CCO that leverages Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithms. Inspired by the integration of state preparation and evolution in data re-uploading, we propose a context re-uploading phase-separator that jointly captures the complex relations among contexts, uncertain coefficients, and optimal solutions. This allows a contextual encoder to be seamlessly integrated within a quantum surrogate policy, enabling joint end-to-end training with a stationarity guarantee. Exploiting an optimization-aware structure grounded in physical principles that classical methods cannot readily leverage, our approach demonstrates practicality by directly training on task loss despite the discreteness and nonconvexity, while avoiding calls to NP-hard optimization solvers. QEL empirically achieves competitive performance while requiring substantially fewer parameters than classical benchmarks, highlighting its industrial-level potential for the future quantum era.

AI.tldr: QEL introduces a quantum end-to-end learning framework for contextual combinatorial optimization using QAOA with a context re-uploading phase-separator, achieving competitive performance with fewer parameters than classical methods.
AI.motivation: Contextual combinatorial optimization (CCO) is critical for decision-making under uncertainty but remains challenging; existing classical methods struggle with scalability and optimization complexity.
AI.method: Proposes Quantum End-to-End Learning (QEL) using Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithms with a context re-uploading phase-separator that integrates a contextual encoder into a quantum surrogate policy, enabling joint end-to-end training with stationarity guarantees.
AI.result: Achieves competitive performance while requiring substantially fewer parameters than classical benchmarks; demonstrates practicality by training directly on task loss without calling NP-hard solvers.
AI.conclusion: QEL shows industrial-level potential for the quantum era, leveraging physical principles classical methods cannot readily exploit.

title: Mechanism of Efficacy in QAOA for Random k-SAT: From Adiabatic Manifold to Sublinear Parameter Optimization
summary:
The Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (QAOA) is a leading candidate for demonstrating quantum advantage on near-term devices, yet the physical origins of its efficacy remain poorly understood. In this work, we study QAOA for random $k$-SAT problems within a universal-mixer $k$-local search framework, establishing a formal correspondence between adiabatic state transfer and the QAOA ansatz. This correspondence yields a rigorous performance guarantee for random instances with clause density $m=O(n^{1+ε})$ and circuit depth $Θ(n^2)$.
  We further investigate the NISQ regime with shallow circuits of depth $p=O(n)$. Surprisingly, the optimal parameters do not become stochastic under depth compression, but instead remain confined to a structured low-dimensional region, which we identify as a smooth adiabatic manifold. Numerical evidence indicates that this manifold persists across different circuit depths and arises from the variational suppression of adiabatic leakage. Based on this structure, we propose the smooth adiabatic-manifold parameterization (SAMP) strategy, transforming parameter optimization from an unstructured high-dimensional search into a guided refinement process. Numerical experiments on random 3-SAT instances show that SAMP achieves sublinear optimization scaling with circuit depth while providing robust zero-cost initialization for deep circuits.

AI.tldr: This paper establishes a formal correspondence between adiabatic state transfer and QAOA for random k-SAT, proving performance guarantees for deep circuits and revealing that optimal QAOA parameters lie on a smooth adiabatic manifold even in the shallow NISQ regime. Based on this structure, the authors propose SAMP, a parameterization strategy that reduces optimization complexity to sublinear scaling with depth.
AI.motivation: The physical origins of QAOA's efficacy remain poorly understood despite its promise for near-term quantum advantage. This work aims to bridge the gap between adiabatic quantum computing and QAOA to provide theoretical guarantees and practical optimization strategies.
AI.method: The authors study QAOA for random k-SAT within a universal-mixer k-local search framework, establishing a formal correspondence between adiabatic state transfer and the QAOA ansatz. They analyze optimal parameters in the NISQ regime (depth p=O(n)) and propose the smooth adiabatic-manifold parameterization (SAMP) strategy.
AI.result: Rigorous performance guarantee for random instances with clause density m=O(n^{1+ε}) and circuit depth Θ(n²). Optimal parameters remain confined to a structured low-dimensional smooth adiabatic manifold, not stochastic. SAMP achieves sublinear optimization scaling with circuit depth while providing robust zero-cost initialization for deep circuits.
AI.conclusion: The adiabatic manifold structure underlying QAOA parameters enables efficient guided optimization, transforming unstructured high-dimensional search into a refinement process with sublinear depth-scaling complexity.

title: Orbital-Angular-Momentum Entangled Photon Emission from Circular Currents in Semiconductor-Superconductor Structures
summary: We theoretically demonstrate that a superconducting circular current induced in a semiconductor results in emission of orbital-angular-momentum (OAM) entangled photon pairs upon carrier recombination. Combining the macroscopic Ginzburg-Landau theory and the microscopic Bardeen-Cooper-Schrieffer (BCS) theory, we investigate the emission of a superconducting light-emitting diode (SLED) with a spatially varying phase profile in the superconducting order parameter. We show that in the active region of the SLED with a circular supercurrent, radiative recombination processes inherit the order parameter phase and result in photon pairs emitted into modes of different OAM quantum numbers. We demonstrate that coherent superposition of superconducting qubit eigenstates can also be mapped onto a coherent superposition of emitted photon states. We also show that other recombination processes due to thermally excited quasi particles do not significantly degrade the state purity. Our results introduce an original scheme for generating OAM-entangled photons enabling a new method of transmitting superconducting qubit information to photonic channels thereby bridging the gap between solid-state and photon-based platforms for quantum communications and information processing.

AI.tldr: The paper demonstrates theoretically that superconducting circular currents in semiconductors can emit photon pairs entangled in orbital angular momentum (OAM) through carrier recombination, proposing a new method to transfer superconducting qubit information to photonic channels.
AI.motivation: To bridge the gap between solid-state superconducting qubit platforms and photonic quantum communication systems by developing a scheme that generates OAM-entangled photon pairs from superconducting circuits.
AI.method: Combines macroscopic Ginzburg-Landau theory with microscopic BCS theory to model a superconducting light-emitting diode (SLED) with a spatially varying phase profile in the superconducting order parameter, analyzing radiative recombination in the presence of a circular supercurrent.
AI.result: Radiative recombination in the SLED active region inherits the order parameter phase, producing photon pairs emitted into modes with different OAM quantum numbers; coherent superposition of superconducting qubit eigenstates maps onto coherent superposition of emitted photon states; thermally excited quasiparticle recombination does not significantly degrade state purity.
AI.conclusion: This work introduces an original scheme for generating OAM-entangled photons, enabling transmission of superconducting qubit information to photonic channels and bridging solid-state and photon-based quantum platforms.

title: Gravitational Entanglement in Optomechanics: Distinguishing Classical and Quantum Models
summary: Observation of gravitationally induced quantum entanglement is often interpreted as a direct evidence of non-classical gravity. While the form and the degree of non-classicality have been rigorously studied from a foundational perspective, classical models reproducing experimental signatures of such entanglement remain underexplored. Motivated by the experimental simplicity, nearly all existing optomechanical approaches assume Gaussian initial states, and due to the weakness of gravity the quantum Newtonian potential is truncated at the second order. However, this regime admits a classical description in terms of the Wigner-Weyl representation, including features typically associated with quantum entanglement. A clear distinction between classical and quantum predictions emerges only beyond this setting. We comprehensively analyze the possibilities and provide operational witnesses for detection of non-classicality via Wigner negativity, and detection of non-quantumness via negativity of the Weyl operator. Our results demonstrate that the experimental requirements on certifying gravitational entanglement are more stringent than previously anticipated.

AI.tldr: Gravitationally induced entanglement experiments using Gaussian states and second-order truncation can be classically mimicked via Wigner-Weyl representation; true quantum signatures require going beyond this regime, making certification of non-classical gravity more demanding than previously thought.
AI.motivation: Classical models that reproduce experimental signatures of gravitationally induced entanglement remain underexplored, despite rigorous foundational studies of non-classical gravity. Most experiments assume Gaussian initial states and truncate the quantum Newtonian potential at second order due to gravity's weakness, but this regime admits classical description.
AI.method: The authors analyze the Wigner-Weyl representation framework to show that Gaussian initial states with second-order truncation admit classical descriptions. They propose operational witnesses: Wigner negativity for detecting non-classicality, and Weyl operator negativity for detecting non-quantumness.
AI.result: The Gaussian regime with second-order truncation cannot distinguish classical from quantum predictions. True non-classical signatures emerge only beyond this setting. Experimental requirements for certifying gravitational entanglement are more stringent than previously anticipated.
AI.conclusion: Certifying genuine quantum gravity via entanglement experiments requires going beyond Gaussian states and second-order approximations, with operational witnesses based on Wigner and Weyl negativity providing clear discrimination.

title: Bowtie VarQTE: A Resource-Efficient Quantum State Preparation Primitive
summary:
The preparation of quantum states is a fundamental requirement for many quantum algorithms. A native route to preparing physically structured states is based on short-time simulation of dynamical processes, such as real or imaginary time evolution. This work presents a resource-efficient framework for the approximation thereof with \textit{bowtie \ac{VarQTE}} which uses classical simulation where possible and quantum resources where necessary. We introduce a framework that leverages existing causal light-cones to minimize quantum resource requirements in the evaluation of gradient and quantum geometric tensor terms by utilizing classical simulation methods for causally relevant subcircuits. This in turn enables exact parameter updates according to McLachlan's variational principle and, thereby, improves numerical stability. We conduct a comparison with a state preparation method that is based on a tensor-network compiled Trotter algorithm: approximate quantum compilation (AQC). In recent work, this approach has shown impressive performance. However, its key-bottleneck is the necessity to have a classical (approximate) representation of the target state. Our numerical experiments indicate that bowtie VarQTE can achieve comparable fidelities without this requirement. We further illustrate how bowtie VarQTE can facilitate a state-preparation pipeline that combines the simulation of imaginary and real time evolution for a sample-based quantum algorithm. In fact, results on 2D systems show how bowtie VarQTE can reduce the quantum requirements compared to standard, sample-based Krylov diagonalization calculations.
  Our results indicate that VarQTE is a promising primitive for the preparation of physically structured quantum states that reduces requirements on quantum resources by leveraging existing structures and the associated possibility of enabling classical simulations.

AI.tldr: Bowtie VarQTE is a resource-efficient framework for quantum state preparation that combines classical simulation (within causal light-cones) with quantum resources, achieving comparable fidelities to tensor-network compiled Trotter methods without requiring a classical representation of the target state.
AI.motivation: Quantum state preparation is essential for many quantum algorithms. Existing methods like approximate quantum compilation (AQC) require a classical (approximate) representation of the target state, which is a key bottleneck. There is a need for resource-efficient approaches that reduce quantum requirements.
AI.method: Bowtie VarQTE uses classical simulation where possible (within causal light-cones) and quantum resources where necessary. It leverages existing causal light-cones to minimize quantum resource requirements in evaluating gradient and quantum geometric tensor terms. Parameter updates follow McLachlan's variational principle exactly via classical simulation of causally relevant subcircuits.
AI.result: Bowtie VarQTE achieves comparable fidelities to AQC without requiring a classical representation of the target state. It reduces quantum requirements compared to standard sample-based Krylov diagonalization calculations in 2D systems. It facilitates a state-preparation pipeline combining imaginary and real time evolution for sample-based quantum algorithms.
AI.conclusion: VarQTE is a promising primitive for preparing physically structured quantum states that reduces quantum resource requirements by exploiting existing structures and enabling classical simulations where possible.

title: Halving the cost of QROM
summary: Table lookup, often referred to as quantum read only memory (QROM), is one of the most widely used subroutines in quantum algorithms, and constitutes the majority share of algorithmic overheads in most practical applications of quantum computers. It involves the coherent loading of $N$ bitstrings of length $b$ in superposition, and naively has a non-Clifford cost of $N$ Toffolis. It is known that given access to $b\, λ$ dirty qubits, one can reduce the Toffoli cost of QROM to $2\frac{N}λ + 4b(λ- 1)$. In this work, we first present an optimization to reduce this cost to $2\frac{N}λ + 2b(λ- 1) + 2λ-6$ by replacing the ``SelectSwap" architecture with ``SelectCopy". We then provide a further optimization for the qubit-constrained regime where the Toffoli cost is typically $\sim 2\frac{N}λ$, and reduce it to $\sim (1+\frac{1}{b})\frac{N}λ$, cutting the cost by approximately $50\%$ and effectively matching the performance of clean-qubit QROM using dirty qubits for practical values of $b$. Lastly, we provide a parametric family of methods that allow the interpolation of the prefactor of the $\frac{N}λ $ term from $2$ to ($\, 1+\frac{1}{b}\,$) to obtain the best cost for different qubit availability regimes.

AI.tldr: This paper presents optimizations to reduce the Toffoli cost of quantum read-only memory (QROM) table lookups, particularly in dirty qubit regimes, by introducing "SelectCopy" architecture and achieving up to ~50% cost reduction, matching clean-qubit performance for practical parameters.
AI.motivation: QROM (table lookup) is a dominant subroutine in quantum algorithms, accounting for the majority of non-Clifford overhead in practical quantum computations. Reducing its cost is critical for feasible quantum computing.
AI.method: The authors first replace the "SelectSwap" architecture with "SelectCopy" to reduce Toffoli cost from $2N/λ + 4b(λ-1)$ to $2N/λ + 2b(λ-1) + 2λ-6$. They further optimize for qubit-constrained regimes to reduce cost from ~$2N/λ$ to ~$(1+1/b)N/λ$, and provide a parametric family interpolating between these prefactors.
AI.result: The optimized dirty-qubit QROM achieves approximately 50% cost reduction, effectively matching clean-qubit QROM performance for practical bitlength values $b$. The prefactor of the $N/λ$ term is reduced from 2 to $1+1/b$.
AI.conclusion: The proposed optimizations significantly lower the Toffoli overhead of QROM in dirty qubit settings, with a tunable family of methods to balance cost across different qubit availability scenarios.

title: Forced Gap Post-Selection for Quantum LDPC Codes and their Operations
summary: We develop a simple and general post-selection strategy for high-rate quantum codes that is transferrable across decoders. After an initial baseline run, the decoder is re-run once per logical observable, and forced in these latter runs to provide a solution where the given observable has the complementary outcome. Shots are rejected that find logically complementary solutions with similar likelihoods compared to the baseline. Using the Relay-BP decoder, we benchmark the strategy on the $72$-qubit and $144$-qubit bivariate bicycle codes, as well as surgery gadgets for the latter. In comparison to previous post-selection strategies, our results offer an improved logical error rate by over a factor of $4$ on the same circuit and physical error rate, and at the same rate of post-selection. Our strategies are also lightweight, relying only on FPGA-friendly belief propagation, whereas the previous best used repeated rounds of a high-latency BP-OSD decoder.

AI.tldr: A simple, decoder-agnostic post-selection strategy for quantum codes that re-runs the decoder per logical observable with forced complementary outcomes, rejecting ambiguous shots; achieves >4x improvement in logical error rate over prior methods at the same post-selection rate using lightweight belief propagation on bivariate bicycle codes.
AI.motivation: To improve logical error rates in quantum error correction without increasing hardware overhead or requiring high-latency decoders, by developing a post-selection strategy that is simple, general, and transferrable across different decoders.
AI.method: After a baseline decoding run, the decoder is re-run once per logical observable with forced complementary outcome; shots where the baseline and forced-run solutions have similar likelihoods are rejected. Benchmarking uses the Relay-BP decoder on 72- and 144-qubit bivariate bicycle codes and surgery gadgets.
AI.result: Over 4x improvement in logical error rate compared to previous post-selection strategies at the same circuit and physical error rate and same post-selection rate; the approach is lightweight, relying only on FPGA-friendly belief propagation rather than high-latency BP-OSD.
AI.conclusion: The proposed post-selection strategy provides a practical, efficient, and decoder-agnostic way to significantly reduce logical error rates in high-rate quantum codes with minimal computational overhead.

title: Resource generation and dynamical complexities in open random quantum circuits
summary: Realistic quantum devices are inherently open and often involve environments with memory. Here, we investigate quantum resource generation in two classes of random circuits, namely, memoryless open and memoryful open random circuits, and compare their behavior with the well-explored random unitary circuit model. We show that environmental memory qualitatively alters the dynamics: while unitary and memoryful circuits exhibit sustained growth and saturation of entanglement and non-stabilizerness (magic); memoryless dynamics leads to a distinct behavior where entanglement decays to zero after transient growth, even though non-stabilizerness remains non-zero, indicating the persistence of nonclassical features beyond entanglement. Consistently, Krylov complexity reveals suppressed spreading of quantum states in memoryless circuits, in contrast to strong growth in unitary and memoryful dynamics, which saturates at the maximum value. Finally, we show that memoryful circuits more effectively approach low-order quantum-state k-designs than the other two circuits. Closed dynamics are therefore usually the most resource-generating, but are ideal; realistic dynamics are open and seem to generate less, but if they possess memory, they can sometimes even outdo closed dynamics.

AI.tldr: The paper compares quantum resource generation (entanglement, non-stabilizerness, Krylov complexity) across three random circuit types: unitary (closed), memoryless open, and memoryful open circuits. Memoryful circuits resemble unitary behavior with sustained growth, while memoryless circuits show entanglement decay despite persistent non-stabilizerness. Memoryful circuits can sometimes outperform closed dynamics in generating quantum resources.
AI.motivation: Realistic quantum devices are inherently open systems often coupled to environments with memory. Understanding how environmental memory affects quantum resource generation (entanglement, magic, complexity) is crucial for practical quantum information processing.
AI.method: The authors investigate three classes of random circuits: (1) random unitary circuits (closed), (2) memoryless open random circuits, and (3) memoryful open random circuits. They analyze entanglement entropy, non-stabilizerness (magic), Krylov complexity, and k-design formation properties across these circuit types.
AI.result: Memoryless open circuits show transient entanglement growth followed by decay to zero, while non-stabilizerness remains non-zero. Memoryful open circuits exhibit sustained entanglement and magic growth similar to unitary circuits. Krylov complexity shows suppressed state spreading in memoryless circuits. Memoryful circuits achieve low-order quantum-state k-designs more effectively than the other two types.
AI.conclusion: Environmental memory qualitatively alters quantum resource dynamics. While closed dynamics are typically the most resource-generating, memoryful open circuits can sometimes outperform closed dynamics, demonstrating that realistic open systems with memory can be advantageous for quantum information tasks.

title: Sampling Noise and Optimized Measurement Distribution in Imaginary-Time Quantum Dynamics Simulations
summary: Variational quantum dynamics simulations (VQDS) provide a promising route to simulate real- and imaginary-time quantum dynamics on noisy intermediate-scale quantum devices using fixed-depth circuits. However, their practical performance is strongly limited by sampling noise arising from a finite number of circuit measurements. In this work, we systematically investigate the impact of sampling noise on VQDS, with a focus on ground-state preparation in one-dimensional Ising spin models using imaginary time evolution. We compare different regularization strategies for stabilizing the equations of motion and show that Tikhonov regularization provides robust performance in noisy imaginary-time evolution. We then benchmark measurement-distribution strategies that allocate shots by minimizing a cost function that characterizes the error in solving the equation of motion. Using noisy circuit simulations, we demonstrate that such optimized shot allocation can significantly improve state fidelity and reduce the total measurement cost by more than a factor of two compared to uniform shot distributions. We observe that the best results are found if a sufficiently large number of measurements is guaranteed for all circuits, suggesting that a finite fraction of shots should be distributed evenly. Our results provide practical guidelines for implementing measurement-efficient variational quantum dynamics and ground-state preparation on near-term quantum hardware.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates how sampling noise affects variational quantum dynamics simulations (VQDS) and demonstrates that optimized shot allocation, combined with Tikhonov regularization, can improve state fidelity and reduce measurement costs by over 50% compared to uniform shot distributions for ground-state preparation in Ising spin models.
AI.motivation: Variational quantum dynamics simulations (VQDS) are promising for simulating quantum dynamics on noisy intermediate-scale quantum (NISQ) devices, but their performance is strongly limited by sampling noise from finite measurement budgets. The authors aim to understand and mitigate this noise to make VQDS practically viable.
AI.method: The authors systematically investigate sampling noise impact on VQDS using imaginary time evolution for ground-state preparation in 1D Ising spin models. They compare regularization strategies (Tikhonov regularization) and benchmark measurement-distribution strategies that allocate shots by minimizing a cost function characterizing the equation-of-motion error, using noisy circuit simulations.
AI.result: Tikhonov regularization provides robust performance in noisy imaginary-time evolution. Optimized shot allocation significantly improves state fidelity and reduces total measurement cost by more than a factor of two compared to uniform shot distributions. Best results require a sufficiently large minimum number of measurements for all circuits.
AI.conclusion: The study provides practical guidelines for implementing measurement-efficient variational quantum dynamics and ground-state preparation on near-term quantum hardware, emphasizing that a finite fraction of shots should be distributed evenly while optimizing the remainder.

title: Interpreting Bohm quantum potentials in Computing quantum waves exactly from classical action
comment: Bohm quantum potential, Madelung equation, Computing quantum waves exactly from classical action, G. Vattay, arXiv:2605.02621 [quant-ph]
summary: The recent arXiv posting [11], commenting on the paper [7], argues that the proof of Lemma 3.1 in [7] is missing the Bohm quantum potential [1, 2] of the Madelung p.d.e. [9]. This short technical note extends the proof of Lemma 3.1 to introduce a Bohm quantum potential explicitly, and then shows why this term can be assumed to be zero in the wave construction, without loss of generality. The continuity p.d.e. and the Hamilton-Jacobi p.d.e., extended by the Bohm potential, are undisputed. However, the actual action and density solutions depend on their initialization at t = 0. In [7], this initialization is motivated by the Feynman kernel [4], which is fundamentally different from the standard initialization of the Madelung solution [9]. This in turn leads to different action and density solutions, and explains why in one case the Bohm quantum potential disappears and in the other does not. The resulting overall wave, however, is independent of this computational initialization.

AI.tldr: This technical note extends Lemma 3.1 from [7] by explicitly incorporating the Bohm quantum potential, then shows this term can be set to zero in the wave construction without loss of generality, due to differences in initialization (Feynman kernel vs. Madelung standard initialization).
AI.motivation: To address the critique in [11] that Lemma 3.1 of [7] omits the Bohm quantum potential, and to resolve the apparent discrepancy between the two initialization approaches.
AI.method: Extends the proof of Lemma 3.1 to include the Bohm quantum potential explicitly, then demonstrates that the term vanishes under the Feynman kernel-based initialization used in [7], unlike the standard Madelung initialization.
AI.result: The Bohm quantum potential disappears under the Feynman kernel initialization but not under the standard Madelung initialization; however, the overall wave function is independent of the initialization choice.
AI.conclusion: The Bohm quantum potential can be assumed zero in the wave construction of [7] without loss of generality, as the overall wave function is invariant under different initialization schemes.

title: Compact narrowband photon-pair generation by slow-light spectral engineering
summary: Efficiently generating photon pairs with high heralding efficiency and high single photon purity that are bandwidth matched to quantum emitters, quantum memories, and other matter-based qubits is critical for quantum networking applications. However, nonlinear optics-based sources require substantial spectral engineering to overcome the orders of magnitude bandwidth mismatch between those sources and qubit systems. A popular solution is cavity-enhanced spontaneous parametric down conversion (SPDC) where the cavity sets the photon bandwidth and simultaneously enhances the spectral brightness of the SPDC. Bulk, free-space configurations are generally required to achieve the MHz-scale bandwidths required to interface with most qubit systems. Replicating these in scalable integrated photonic architectures is an ongoing challenge due to the much higher propagation losses that limit the size and linewidth of chip-based resonators. We show here how an intra-cavity slow light medium, acting as an ultra-narrow filter, would enable narrowband photon pair generation in broadband cavities with high single photon purity and without compromising the heralding efficiency. We show that such metrics can be readily realized in erbium doped thin-film lithium niobate microrings using realistic design parameters.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes using an intra-cavity slow light medium as an ultra-narrow filter to enable narrowband photon pair generation in broadband integrated photonic cavities, achieving high heralding efficiency and single photon purity without spectral engineering constraints. The scheme is shown feasible in erbium-doped thin-film lithium niobate microrings.
AI.motivation: Efficiently generating narrowband photon pairs with high heralding efficiency and purity that are bandwidth-matched to quantum emitters, memories, and matter-based qubits is critical for quantum networking. Nonlinear optics sources suffer from orders-of-magnitude bandwidth mismatch with qubit systems, and while cavity-enhanced SPDC in bulk free-space configurations can achieve MHz-scale bandwidths, replicating this in scalable integrated photonic architectures remains an ongoing challenge due to high propagation losses limiting chip-based resonator linewidths.
AI.method: The authors propose integrating an intra-cavity slow light medium within a broadband integrated cavity (erbium-doped thin-film lithium niobate microring) to act as an ultra-narrow spectral filter. This approach enables narrowband photon pair generation without requiring the cavity itself to have a narrow linewidth, thereby circumventing the propagation loss limitations of integrated resonators.
AI.result: The proposed scheme enables narrowband photon pair generation in broadband integrated cavities with high single photon purity and without compromising heralding efficiency. The metrics are shown to be achievable using realistic design parameters in erbium-doped thin-film lithium niobate microrings.
AI.conclusion: Intra-cavity slow light media provide a viable path to realizing narrowband SPDC photon sources in scalable integrated photonic platforms, overcoming the fundamental trade-off between cavity linewidth and propagation loss that has hindered chip-based implementations.

title: One-Dimensional Nonlinear Quantum Walks
summary: We explore a continuous-time quantum walk starting at a single vertex on the discrete path and cycle with a cubic nonlinearity. Such nonlinearities arise in Bose-Einstein condensates described by the Gross-Pitaevskii equation or by nonlinear optical waveguide arrays. We analytically prove that the nonlinear quantum walk can be trapped to arbitrary fidelity depending on the coefficient of the nonlinear term. This contrasts with linear quantum walks, which are known for spreading quickly in one dimension. We propose that this trapping can be used for timing in quantum state transfer, where a qubit is held at a node until it is ready to be transferred, and it can also be held again at the receiving node. This scheme can also be interpreted as a form of quantum memory, with the trap and transfer corresponding to the storage and release of quantum information.

AI.tldr: This paper demonstrates that a nonlinear continuous-time quantum walk on discrete graphs (path and cycle) can trap a quantum walker at a single vertex with arbitrary fidelity, unlike linear quantum walks which spread quickly. This trapping mechanism is proposed for timing control in quantum state transfer and as a form of quantum memory.
AI.motivation: Linear quantum walks spread rapidly in one dimension, limiting control. The authors seek to exploit cubic nonlinearity (from Bose-Einstein condensates or nonlinear optics) to achieve trapping, enabling precise timing and memory functions in quantum information processing.
AI.method: The authors analytically study a continuous-time quantum walk with a cubic nonlinear term on discrete path and cycle graphs, starting from a single vertex. They analyze the trapping fidelity as a function of the nonlinear coefficient.
AI.result: The nonlinear quantum walk can be trapped to arbitrary fidelity depending on the nonlinear coefficient, in stark contrast to linear quantum walks which spread quickly in one dimension.
AI.conclusion: The trapping effect can be used for timing in quantum state transfer (holding a qubit at a node until ready to transfer) and as quantum memory (storage and release of quantum information).

title: Mean-field and fluctuation dynamics in off-resonant two-mode atom-field interactions
summary: We study a two-level system coupled to two quantized electromagnetic modes within the Jaynes-Cummings framework. While the single-mode model is exactly solvable due to its conserved excitation number, yielding finite-dimensional invariant subspaces, the two-mode model extension presents a fundamental challenge: although the total excitation number remains conserved, each invariant subspace is infinite-dimensional, preventing a closed-form analytical solution. Our scheme separates the dynamics into a dominant, exactly solvable semiclassical component, the atom interacting with the mean fields of both modes, and treats the remaining quantum fluctuations through a sequence of unitary transformations that preserve essential quantum features. We validate our approach through direct comparison with numerical solutions, focusing on the non-resonant regime where multiple detunings give rise to rich interference effects and multi-timescale dynamics inaccessible to standard approximations. The method accurately reproduces atomic inversion, field observables, and fidelity over relevant timescales, while remaining computationally efficient.

AI.tldr: A method combining semiclassical decomposition and unitary transformations is proposed to solve the two-mode Jaynes-Cummings model, where infinite-dimensional invariant subspaces prevent exact analytical solutions. The approach accurately reproduces dynamics in the non-resonant regime and remains computationally efficient.
AI.motivation: The two-mode Jaynes-Cummings model, unlike the single-mode case, has infinite-dimensional invariant subspaces despite conserved excitation number, preventing closed-form analytical solutions. Standard approximations fail in the non-resonant regime with multiple detunings.
AI.method: The dynamics are separated into a dominant semiclassical component (atom interacting with mean fields of both modes) and quantum fluctuations treated via a sequence of unitary transformations that preserve essential quantum features.
AI.result: The method accurately reproduces atomic inversion, field observables, and fidelity over relevant timescales when validated against numerical solutions, particularly in the non-resonant regime with rich interference effects and multi-timescale dynamics.
AI.conclusion: The proposed scheme provides an accurate and computationally efficient approach for the two-mode Jaynes-Cummings model, overcoming the limitations of standard approximations in regimes with multiple detunings.

title: PUBO Formulation for MST and Application to Optimum-Path Forest
summary: The Optimum-Path Forest is a graph-based framework for designing classifiers that exploit inter-sample connectivity. A particular variant constructs decision boundaries based on prototypes computed by a Minimum Spanning Tree (MST) over the training data, which might become prohibitive for large-scale datasets. In this context, Quantum Machine Learning has emerged as a promising approach to overcome the high computational burden of combinatorial problems. We propose a quantum-inspired approach for prototype selection in OPF classifiers by reformulating the MST problem as a Polynomial Unconstrained Binary Optimization (PUBO) task and further employing the Feedback-Based Quantum Optimization (FALQON) algorithm for Hamiltonian minimization. The PUBO formulation reduces the need for qubits and eliminates the need for auxiliary variables, thereby addressing scalability constraints in current quantum hardware. Experiments on real-world datasets demonstrate that the FALQON-optimized MST achieves accuracies comparable to those of the classical Prim's algorithm while maintaining prototype quality. While FALQON occasionally reached local minima, it did not significantly impact the accuracy of the prototype selection process.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a quantum-inspired approach for prototype selection in Optimum-Path Forest classifiers, reformulating the Minimum Spanning Tree problem as a Polynomial Unconstrained Binary Optimization task solved via the Feedback-Based Quantum Optimization (FALQON) algorithm, achieving comparable accuracy to classical methods with reduced qubit requirements.
AI.motivation: The Minimum Spanning Tree computation for prototype selection in OPF classifiers becomes computationally prohibitive for large-scale datasets. The authors aim to leverage Quantum Machine Learning to overcome this computational burden while addressing scalability constraints of current quantum hardware.
AI.method: The authors reformulate the MST problem as a Polynomial Unconstrained Binary Optimization (PUBO) task, eliminating auxiliary variables and reducing qubit requirements. They employ the Feedback-Based Quantum Optimization (FALQON) algorithm for Hamiltonian minimization to perform prototype selection in OPF classifiers.
AI.result: Experiments on real-world datasets show that the FALQON-optimized MST achieves accuracies comparable to the classical Prim's algorithm while maintaining prototype quality. FALQON occasionally reached local minima but this did not significantly impact prototype selection accuracy.
AI.conclusion: The proposed quantum-inspired approach offers a scalable alternative for prototype selection in OPF classifiers by reducing qubit demands and eliminating auxiliary variables, achieving competitive performance with classical methods despite occasional convergence to local minima.

title: WSi weak link element with a non-sinusoidal current-phase relation
summary: Nonlinearity is an essential ingredient for encoding quantum states with non-uniform energy spacing, implementing coherent quantum gates, reading out qubits, amplifying, and mixing electromagnetic signals. In this work, we demonstrate the nonlinear behavior of a constriction fabricated from an amorphous, high-kinetic inductance material, tungsten silicide, embedded in a three-dimensional RF-SQUID. We find that the results are consistent with the weak link behaving as a Josephson junction with a sawtooth-like current-phase relation or a quantum phase slip element. Finally, we measure relaxation times of the metastable, persistent-current states trapped in the local minima of the potential.

AI.tldr: A constriction made of amorphous tungsten silicide in a 3D RF-SQUID exhibits nonlinear behavior consistent with a Josephson junction having a sawtooth current-phase relation or a quantum phase slip element, and relaxation times of metastable persistent-current states were measured.
AI.motivation: Nonlinearity is essential for encoding quantum states with non-uniform energy spacing, implementing coherent quantum gates, qubit readout, signal amplification, and mixing. The work aims to demonstrate nonlinear behavior in a high-kinetic inductance constriction as a potential alternative to conventional Josephson junctions.
AI.method: A constriction was fabricated from amorphous tungsten silicide (a high-kinetic inductance material) and embedded in a three-dimensional RF-SQUID. The nonlinear response was characterized and compared to models of a weak link with a sawtooth-like current-phase relation or a quantum phase slip element. Relaxation times of metastable persistent-current states were measured.
AI.result: The nonlinear behavior observed is consistent with either a Josephson junction exhibiting a sawtooth current-phase relation or a quantum phase slip element. Relaxation times of metastable persistent-current states trapped in local potential minima were successfully measured.
AI.conclusion: A constriction in amorphous tungsten silicide can serve as a nonlinear quantum element, offering an alternative platform for superconducting quantum circuits.

title: Entangling Power: A Probe of Symmetry and Integrability in Quantum Many-Body Systems
comment: A vibe-coding project; 27 pages, 9 figures, and 4 appendices
summary: The entangling power of a unitary operator quantifies its ability to generate entanglement from product states and provides a natural probe of quantum many-body dynamics. Entanglement extremization at points of enhanced symmetry has previously been observed in high-energy scattering. In this work we compute the time-averaged entangling power of anisotropic Heisenberg spin chains across two-site models and finite-size systems, as well as the entangling power of the two-magnon $S$-matrix in the thermodynamic limit. For two-site models we establish a monotonic hierarchy: the entangling power decreases as the symmetry group grows, reaching its minimum at the $SU(2)$ XXX point. Finite-size XXZ chains exhibit sharp dips at the $SU(2)$ points $Δ=\pm 1$ and the free-fermion point $Δ=0$, with the free-fermion dip decaying much more slowly with system size. In the thermodynamic limit, we decompose the two-magnon $S$-matrix into quantum logic gates -- Identity, SWAP, and $σ_z\otimesσ_z$ -- and show that the entangling power vanishes for all scattering energies at the $SU(2)$ points, where the $S$-matrix reduces to the Identity gate, while the free-fermion point achieves the maximum -- the opposite of the finite-size many-body behavior. The entangling power can serve as an {\em operator} diagnostic for symmetry and selected aspects of integrability in quantum simulations of spin-chain dynamics.

AI.tldr: This paper calculates the time-averaged entangling power of anisotropic Heisenberg spin chains and the two-magnon S-matrix, finding that entangling power decreases with increasing symmetry (minimum at SU(2) XXX point), exhibits sharp dips at Δ=±1 (SU(2)) and Δ=0 (free-fermion) in finite chains, but in the thermodynamic limit the two-magnon S-matrix entangling power vanishes at SU(2) points and maximizes at the free-fermion point — opposite to finite-size behavior.
AI.motivation: To understand how entangling power — a quantitative measure of a unitary operator's ability to generate entanglement — behaves across symmetry groups and system sizes in quantum many-body spin systems, and whether it can serve as an operator diagnostic for symmetry and integrability.
AI.method: Compute time-averaged entangling power for two-site anisotropic Heisenberg models, finite-size XXZ chains, and the two-magnon S-matrix in the thermodynamic limit; decompose the S-matrix into Identity, SWAP, and σ_z⊗σ_z gates.
AI.result: Two-site models show monotonic hierarchy (entangling power decreases with larger symmetry groups, minimum at SU(2) XXX point). Finite-size XXZ chains show sharp dips at SU(2) points Δ=±1 and free-fermion point Δ=0, with free-fermion dip decaying more slowly. In thermodynamic limit, two-magnon S-matrix entangling power vanishes at SU(2) points (S-matrix reduces to Identity) but achieves maximum at free-fermion point — opposite to finite-size behavior.
AI.conclusion: Entangling power serves as an operator-level diagnostic for symmetry and aspects of integrability in quantum simulations of spin-chain dynamics.

title: Strongly-coupled non-Markovian waveguide QED with input-output HEOM
summary: We consider the problem of modeling a single qubit in contact with a one-dimensional waveguide beyond the standard perturbative and Markovian approximations. Using the recently developed input-output hierarchical equations of motion (io-HEOM), we investigate multiple examples of such waveguides, characterized by different spectral densities. Our examples highlight that the io-HEOM method can accurately capture non-Markovianity in waveguide QED from two distinct origins. The first source of non-Markovianity is spatially non-local coupling between the qubit and the waveguide. By examining two examples with non-local coupling, we show how the coupling function affects the steady-state bound photons, and demonstrate the release of these photons when the qubit energy is quenched. The second source of non-Markovianity is non-linear dispersion. We illustrate this scenario using the example of a cavity array with point-like coupling, where the non-linear dispersion leads to persistent oscillations due to Van Hove singularities in the spectral density.

AI.tldr: The paper uses the input-output hierarchical equations of motion (io-HEOM) method to model a qubit coupled to a 1D waveguide beyond standard approximations, capturing non-Markovianity from two sources: (1) spatially non-local coupling, and (2) non-linear dispersion.
AI.motivation: To model a single qubit in contact with a one-dimensional waveguide beyond the standard perturbative and Markovian approximations.
AI.method: Input-output hierarchical equations of motion (io-HEOM) method, applied to waveguides with different spectral densities.
AI.result: The io-HEOM method accurately captures non-Markovianity from spatially non-local coupling (showing effects on steady-state bound photons and their release upon qubit energy quenching) and from non-linear dispersion (leading to persistent oscillations due to Van Hove singularities).
AI.conclusion: The io-HEOM method is effective for studying non-Markovian waveguide QED beyond perturbative and Markovian limits.

title: Precision and Privacy in Distributed Quantum Sensing: A Quantum Fisher Information Duality
summary: We establish a quantum Fisher information (QFI) duality for distributed quantum sensor networks with local phase encoding. For any $N$-qubit probe state, where $N$ denotes the number of sensors, $F_Q(\boldsymbol{w}^\top \boldsymbolθ) + F_Q(\boldsymbol{v}^\top \boldsymbolθ) \leq N$ for all unit orthogonal sensing directions $\boldsymbol{w}$ and $\boldsymbol{v}$, with equality for all equatorial states when $N=2$ and for Greenberger--Horne--Zeilinger (GHZ) states when $N\geq 2$. Heisenberg-limited precision for direction $\boldsymbol{w}$, $F_Q(\boldsymbol{w}^\top \boldsymbolθ)=N$, saturates the bound and simultaneously forces zero QFI for all other independent directions. This can be interpreted as the condition for parameter privacy in distributed quantum sensing: attaining Heisenberg-limited precision for the sensing target renders all alternative privacy-intrusive estimations impossible.

AI.tldr: The paper establishes a quantum Fisher information (QFI) duality bound for distributed quantum sensor networks: for any N-qubit probe state, F_Q(w^T θ) + F_Q(v^T θ) ≤ N for orthogonal sensing directions w and v. Heisenberg-limited sensing (QFI=N) in one direction forces zero QFI in all orthogonal directions, providing a quantum privacy guarantee against intrusive estimations.
AI.motivation: To establish a fundamental trade-off (duality) in quantum Fisher information for distributed quantum sensor networks, and to show that Heisenberg-limited precision in one sensing direction automatically enforces parameter privacy by suppressing QFI in all other independent directions.
AI.method: The paper derives a QFI duality inequality for distributed quantum sensor networks with local phase encoding. It proves that for any N-qubit probe state, the sum of QFIs along two orthogonal sensing directions is bounded by N, with equality conditions identified for equatorial states (N=2) and GHZ states (N≥2).
AI.result: F_Q(w^T θ) + F_Q(v^T θ) ≤ N for all unit orthogonal w, v; Heisenberg-limited sensing (QFI=N) in direction w forces zero QFI in all other independent directions; GHZ and equatorial states saturate the bound.
AI.conclusion: The QFI duality reveals a fundamental privacy-preserving mechanism: achieving Heisenberg-limited precision for a target sensing parameter automatically prevents estimation of any other independent parameters, thus providing inherent parameter privacy in distributed quantum sensing.

title: Generalized quantum Stein's lemma for mixed sources
summary: The generalized quantum Stein's lemma characterizes the optimal asymptotic exponent of the type-II error in quantum hypothesis testing for an independent and identically distributed (IID) null hypothesis against a composite alternative hypothesis. Classically, a probabilistic mixture of IID sources arises as a natural generalization of IID sources, and, in the non-composite setting, the optimal type-II error exponent in hypothesis testing for such classical mixed sources is known to be characterized concisely by the worst-case component of the mixture. In this work, we extend these foundational results to composite quantum hypothesis testing where the null hypothesis is a mixed source, i.e., a probabilistic mixture of IID quantum states, and the alternative hypothesis is composite as in the generalized quantum Stein's lemma. When the type-I error vanishes asymptotically, we characterize the optimal type-II error exponent of this composite quantum hypothesis testing problem in terms of the worst-case component of the mixture, by developing techniques for the non-commutative quantum setting inspired by the classical information-spectrum analysis. We also show that the analogous characterization does not hold in general for a fixed nonzero type-I error threshold, by providing a counterexample beyond the vanishing type-I error regime. These results clarify the applicability of the generalized quantum Stein's lemma to highly non-IID null hypotheses arising from arbitrary finite probabilistic mixtures of IID quantum states.

AI.tldr: This paper extends the generalized quantum Stein's lemma to composite quantum hypothesis testing where the null hypothesis is a probabilistic mixture of IID quantum states (mixed source). The optimal type-II error exponent is characterized by the worst-case component when type-I error vanishes, but this characterization fails for fixed nonzero type-I error thresholds.
AI.motivation: To extend foundational results on optimal type-II error exponents from classical mixed-source hypothesis testing and the generalized quantum Stein's lemma to the composite quantum setting where the null hypothesis is a probabilistic mixture of IID quantum states, and to understand the applicability limits of the generalized quantum Stein's lemma for non-IID null hypotheses.
AI.method: The authors develop non-commutative quantum techniques inspired by classical information-spectrum analysis to handle the composite hypothesis testing problem where the null hypothesis is a mixed source (probabilistic mixture of IID quantum states) and the alternative is composite.
AI.result: When type-I error vanishes asymptotically, the optimal type-II error exponent is characterized by the worst-case component of the mixture. However, this characterization does not hold for fixed nonzero type-I error thresholds, demonstrated via a counterexample.
AI.conclusion: The results clarify the applicability of the generalized quantum Stein's lemma to highly non-IID null hypotheses arising from finite probabilistic mixtures of IID quantum states, showing that the worst-case component characterization holds only in the vanishing type-I error regime.

title: Multi-Qubit Entanglement of Unit Cell Pairs in SiMOS
summary: Spin qubits in silicon-MOS (SiMOS) quantum dots have recently demonstrated compatibility with existing industry standard CMOS fabrication techniques. These devices have routinely achieved single- and two-qubit gate fidelities above 99% and demonstrated highly entangled two-qubit Bell states in isolated double quantum dot (DQD) unit cells, however coupling between unit cells has remained challenging. In this work, we present a two unit cell, four-qubit SiMOS processor with universal controllability and fully parallelised state initialisation and readout. We use this processor to generate maximally entangled three-qubit states, including the Greenberger-Horne-Zeilinger (GHZ) state, and certify multipartite entanglement through violation of the classical Mermin-witness bound. By using a fully symmetric dynamically decoupled gate sequence to create our entangled states, we are able to preserve the lifetime of the entanglement beyond $T_2^*$, to a time limited instead by $T_2^\textrm{Hahn}$. These demonstrations pave a road to the scalable operation of larger SiMOS processors, and achieving high purity, long-lived multi-qubit entangled states in them.

AI.tldr: A four-qubit SiMOS quantum processor with two unit cells demonstrates universal controllability, parallelised state initialisation/readout, and generates maximally entangled three-qubit GHZ states. Using dynamically decoupled gate sequences, entanglement lifetime is extended beyond $T_2^*$ to $T_2^\text{Hahn}$, paving the way for scalable SiMOS quantum processors.
AI.motivation: Existing SiMOS quantum dot devices achieve high-fidelity single/two-qubit gates and entangled Bell states in isolated double quantum dot unit cells, but coupling between unit cells remains challenging, limiting scalability to larger multi-qubit processors.
AI.method: A two-unit-cell, four-qubit SiMOS processor with full parallelised state initialisation and readout is fabricated using industry-compatible CMOS techniques. A fully symmetric dynamically decoupled gate sequence is employed to generate three-qubit entangled states, protecting entanglement coherence beyond $T_2^*$ to the longer $T_2^\text{Hahn}$ timescale.
AI.result: Maximally entangled three-qubit GHZ states are generated and multipartite entanglement is certified via violation of the classical Mermin-witness bound. Entanglement lifetime is extended beyond $T_2^*$ to $T_2^\text{Hahn}$ using dynamically decoupled sequences.
AI.conclusion: Scalable operation of larger SiMOS processors is achievable, and high-purity, long-lived multi-qubit entangled states can be realised in these systems.

title: Circuits of Quantum Hashing and Quantum Fourier Transform for a Cactus as a Qubit Connectivity Graph
summary: We present a quantum circuit implementation of the quantum hashing algorithm (quantum fingerprinting) for a quantum device with restrictions on the application of two-qubit gates by a qubit connectivity graph. We present an optimization technique for the shallow circuit for quantum hashing in the case of a cactus as a qubit connectivity graph. The algorithm has $O(n^3)$ complexity to build the circuit, where $n$ is the number of qubits and $m$ is the number of connections (edges) in the graph. It is improvement compared to the existing exponential-time algorithm in the case of arbitrary graphs. The algorithm uses solution for the shortest non-simple 1-covering path problem as a subroutine. We present an $O(n^3)$-time solution for this graph-theory problem in the case of a cactus. This result can be interesting independently. The algorithm also used for improving of the quantum circuit for Quantum Fourier Transform.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a quantum circuit implementation of quantum hashing optimized for cactus connectivity graphs, improving from exponential to O(n^3) complexity, with applications to Quantum Fourier Transform.
AI.motivation: To enable efficient quantum circuit implementation of quantum hashing on quantum devices with restricted qubit connectivity graphs, specifically addressing the exponential complexity bottleneck of existing algorithms for arbitrary graphs.
AI.method: The authors propose an O(n^3) optimization technique for constructing shallow quantum hashing circuits on cactus connectivity graphs, using a solution to the shortest non-simple 1-covering path problem as a key subroutine, and extending the approach to improve Quantum Fourier Transform circuits.
AI.result: The algorithm achieves O(n^3) complexity for building the circuit on cactus graphs, a significant improvement over the exponential-time algorithm for arbitrary graphs. Additionally, an O(n^3)-time solution for the shortest non-simple 1-covering path problem on cactus graphs is provided.
AI.conclusion: The work provides a scalable approach to quantum hashing circuit construction under realistic hardware constraints, with independent contributions to graph theory and potential improvements to QFT circuits.

title: Decoy Statebased Time Synchronization
summary: Time synchronization is a crucial requirement in quantum key distribution (QKD)8 protocols, ensuring accurate key generation via the correct assignment of bits of raw key and9 enabling eavesdropping detection via the precise recording of photon statistics. State-of-the-art10 experiments typically use an extra channel to synchronize the clocks of the transmitter and receiver11 via classical signals. In this work, we study the possibility of performing clock synchronization12 via the signals used for the key generation, which are already present in decoy-state-based BB8413 protocols.14 Without altering the protocol in any way, we use the different mean photon numbers of the15 signal and decoy states for time synchronization without a dedicated physical channel capable of16 clock synchronization. The proposed method relies only on the photons sent and received for17 key generation and does not require any change to the QKD protocol. The only change in the18 experiment is on the software level, thus making it very simple to implement.19 We demonstrate clock synchronization method in a simulation of a specific fiber-based QKD20 experiment. Like other decoy-state-based BB84 protocols, it is based on weak coherent pulses.21 In this simulation, we investigate the parameter space to find limits and optimal choices of our22 proposed method.23 In addition to the non-protocol-altering clock synchronization method, we also discuss an24 approach that significantly improves performance in lossy channels by introducing an additional25 decoy state with a very high mean photon number.26 By eliminating the need for an extra channel capable of clock synchronization, both methods27 proposed potentially reduce the complexity and cost of QKD systems and improve their agility

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a clock synchronization method for QKD that uses existing decoy-state signals (different mean photon numbers of signal and decoy states) rather than an extra dedicated physical channel, and also discusses an enhanced approach using an additional high-mean-photon-number decoy state for lossy channels.
AI.motivation: Time synchronization is critical for QKD protocols (accurate key generation and eavesdropping detection), but state-of-the-art experiments typically require an extra channel with classical signals for clock synchronization, adding complexity and cost.
AI.method: The method exploits the different mean photon numbers of signal and decoy states already present in decoy-state-based BB84 protocols for time synchronization, requiring no protocol changes—only software-level modifications. A second method adds an extra decoy state with a very high mean photon number to improve performance in lossy channels.
AI.result: The clock synchronization method was demonstrated via simulation of a fiber-based QKD experiment using weak coherent pulses, with investigation of parameter space to find limits and optimal choices.
AI.conclusion: Both methods eliminate the need for an extra channel capable of clock synchronization, potentially reducing QKD system complexity, cost, and improving agility.

title: Enhancing Phase Estimation in a Hybrid Interferometer via Kerr Nonlinearity and Photon Subtraction
summary: We propose a high-precision phase estimation scheme in a hybrid interferometer by synergistically combining a Kerr nonlinear phase shifter and multi-photon subtraction operations. Using a coherent state and a vacuum state as input resources, we systematically evaluate the phase sensitivity via homodyne detection and analyze the quantum Fisher information as well as the quantum Cramér-Rao bound under both ideal and lossy conditions. Our results show that the joint integration of Kerr nonlinearity and multi-photon subtraction yields remarkable advantages over either technique used alone. The proposed scheme enables the phase sensitivity to surpass the standard quantum limit, exceed the conventional Heisenberg scaling ($1/N$), and approach the super-Heisenberg scaling ($1/N^{2}$)-a direct consequence of Kerr nonlinearity. More precisely, the super-Heisenberg scaling $\propto $ $1/N^{2}$ is the ultimate precision limit permitted by the $k=2$ Kerr nonlinearity and does not violate the fundamental Heisenberg limit for linear phase accumulation. Even under moderate internal photon loss, the system maintains high precision and exhibits enhanced robustness to decoherence. The Kerr nonlinearity introduces an intensity-dependent phase shift proportional to the squared photon number, while multi-photon subtraction tailors non-Gaussian states to strengthen phase information extraction. Compared with existing schemes based on hybrid interferometers or SU(1,1) interferometers, our architecture achieves superior precision and stronger loss resilience. All components are experimentally accessible with current quantum optical technologies. This work provides a promising route for practical high-precision quantum metrology and quantum sensing.

AI.tldr: A hybrid interferometer combining Kerr nonlinear phase shifter and multi-photon subtraction achieves phase sensitivity beyond standard quantum limit, surpassing Heisenberg scaling ($1/N$) and approaching super-Heisenberg scaling ($1/N^2$), with robustness to photon loss and feasibility with current quantum optical technology.
AI.motivation: To overcome the precision limitations of conventional optical interferometry and achieve phase sensitivity beyond standard quantum limit and Heisenberg scaling, by synergistically integrating Kerr nonlinearity and multi-photon subtraction in a hybrid interferometer.
AI.method: Combines a Kerr nonlinear phase shifter with multi-photon subtraction operations in a hybrid interferometer using coherent state and vacuum state inputs; evaluates phase sensitivity via homodyne detection, quantum Fisher information, and quantum Cramér-Rao bound under both ideal and lossy conditions.
AI.result: The scheme surpasses standard quantum limit, exceeds conventional Heisenberg scaling ($1/N$), and approaches super-Heisenberg scaling ($1/N^2$) — the ultimate limit for $k=2$ Kerr nonlinearity; maintains high precision under moderate internal photon loss; outperforms existing hybrid and SU(1,1) interferometers.
AI.conclusion: The synergistic integration of Kerr nonlinearity and multi-photon subtraction offers a practical, loss-resilient route for high-precision quantum metrology, with all components realizable using current quantum optical technologies.

title: Coherent Feedback Cooling of an Ultracoherent Phononic-Crystal Membrane at Room Temperature
summary: Optomechanical systems provide a versatile platform for precision measurements and investigations of fundamental physics, where bringing macroscopic resonators into the quantum regime is a widely pursued goal. Achieving such quantum behavior of solid-state mechanical resonators at room temperature would greatly broaden their applications by removing the need for cryogenic environments. Reaching this goal requires efficient cooling of mechanical motion, among various laser cooling methods, dynamical backaction cooling (DBC) is widely utilized in experiments but fundamentally limited when operating in the sideband-unresolved regime. Coherent feedback cooling (CFC) can overcome this limitation, while avoiding state collapse and the electronic restrictions inherent to measurement-based feedback. Here, we experimentally demonstrate CFC using an ultracoherent density phononic crystal membrane. By combining CFC with strong DBC in a relatively narrow cavity, we achieve a phonon occupation reduction from $5.5\times10^{6}$ to $166\pm7$, corresponding to a cooling factor of $3.3\times10^{4}$ at room temperature, even with current experimental limitations. Our results show the potential of CFC for approaching the ground state of high-$Q$ membranes at room temperature.

AI.tldr: The authors experimentally demonstrate coherent feedback cooling (CFC) combined with dynamical backaction cooling (DBC) to cool a phononic crystal membrane from 5.5×10⁶ to 166±7 phonons (cooling factor ~3.3×10⁴) at room temperature, showing that CFC overcomes the sideband-unresolved limitation of DBC and can approach ground-state cooling of high-Q membranes without cryogenics.
AI.motivation: Bringing macroscopic solid-state mechanical resonators into the quantum regime at room temperature would greatly expand their applications in precision measurements and fundamental physics, but this requires efficient laser cooling that overcomes the fundamental limitations of existing methods like dynamical backaction cooling (DBC) in the sideband-unresolved regime.
AI.method: The authors employ coherent feedback cooling (CFC) combined with strong DBC in a narrow cavity, using an ultracoherent density phononic crystal membrane as the mechanical resonator.
AI.result: Phonon occupation reduced from 5.5×10⁶ to 166±7, achieving a cooling factor of 3.3×10⁴ at room temperature, even with current experimental limitations.
AI.conclusion: CFC shows strong potential for approaching the ground state of high-Q membranes at room temperature by overcoming the sideband-unresolved limitation inherent to DBC, while avoiding state collapse and electronic restrictions of measurement-based feedback.

title: Symmetric dilations of Pauli channels and semigroups
summary: We explore the symmetry properties of Stinespring dilations of single-qubit Pauli channels, addressing both the generic case and the specific examples of phase damping and depolarizing channels. For each scenario, we derive the representation of the Pauli group acting on the Hilbert space of the environment. We then focus on dilations that are continuous in time and driven by a time-independent Hamiltonian, and on collision models that generate a Pauli dynamical semigroup in the limit of fast collisions. First, we complement some recent general results on these types of dilations (M. Cattaneo, Phys. Rev. A 111, 022209 (2025)) with some additions and clarifications, including the case of covariant channels with strongly conserved quantities. Next, we show that the covariance property of Pauli channels impose strong constraints on both the dilation Hamiltonian and the initial state of the environment, and demonstrate how these constraints can be exploited to explicitly construct the time-dependent dilations in all considered cases.
