Our results are relevant for the quantum simulation of Pauli channels via unitary dilations and of Pauli semigroups via collision models, both in the laboratory and on quantum computers.

AI.conclusion: The findings are directly relevant for quantum simulation of Pauli channels via unitary dilations and of Pauli semigroups via collision models, applicable both in laboratory settings and on quantum computers.

title: Symmetry-Protected Fast Relaxation and the Strong Quantum Mpemba Effect
summary: Understanding how symmetry constrains dissipative relaxation in open quantum many-body systems remains a central challenge in nonequilibrium physics. Here we uncover a symmetry-selective Liouvillian mechanism that protects an isolated fast-decay channel in a long-range XXZ spin chain subject to dephasing noise. At the \(SU(2)\)-symmetric point, highly symmetric initial states couple exclusively to an exact Liouvillian eigenmode with decay rate \(λ=-2\), producing universal exponential relaxation independent of system size and interaction range. Breaking the symmetry restores overlap with slow Liouvillian modes and substantially suppresses the relaxation dynamics. This symmetry-filtered mode accessibility naturally gives rise to a strong quantum Mpemba effect, where a state farther from the steady state relaxes anomalously faster than closer thermal states. Our results establish symmetry-protected fast relaxation as a mechanism for controlling nonequilibrium pathways in open quantum systems.

AI.tldr: The paper discovers a symmetry-selective Liouvillian mechanism in a long-range XXZ spin chain with dephasing noise, where at the SU(2)-symmetric point, highly symmetric initial states couple exclusively to a fast-decay mode (λ=-2), producing universal exponential relaxation. Breaking symmetry suppresses relaxation and induces a strong quantum Mpemba effect.
AI.motivation: To understand how symmetry constrains dissipative relaxation in open quantum many-body systems, which remains a central challenge in nonequilibrium physics.
AI.method: Analytical and numerical study of a long-range XXZ spin chain subject to dephasing noise, focusing on the Liouvillian spectrum and mode accessibility at and away from the SU(2)-symmetric point.
AI.result: At SU(2) symmetry, highly symmetric initial states couple exclusively to an exact Liouvillian eigenmode with decay rate λ=-2, yielding universal exponential relaxation independent of system size and interaction range. Breaking symmetry restores overlap with slow modes and suppresses relaxation, producing a strong quantum Mpemba effect.
AI.conclusion: Symmetry-protected fast relaxation provides a mechanism for controlling nonequilibrium pathways in open quantum systems.

title: High-Dimensional Carrier-Assisted Entanglement Purification Based on Mutually Unbiased Bases
summary: Distilling high-dimensional quantum entanglement under realistic, general asymmetric noise remains a formidable challenge. Standard entanglement purification protocols inevitably fail to satisfy convergence constraints under severe asymmetric noise. In this paper, we investigate carrier-assisted entanglement purification protocols, namely CAEPP and mCAEPP, for two-qutrit systems, demonstrating that without adaptive pre-processing, convergence is strictly bottlenecked by marginal $X$-error probabilities. To overcome this limitation, we introduce a deterministic pre-processing scheme based on mutually unbiased bases (MUBs). By actively rotating the qutrit phase space to establish primary-axis error dominance, we rigorously prove that the MUB-adapted mCAEPP deterministically yields unit asymptotic fidelity for any two-qutrit Pauli channel with initial fidelity $p_{00} > 1/3$.

AI.tldr: This paper addresses the challenge of distilling high-dimensional quantum entanglement under asymmetric noise, proposing carrier-assisted protocols (CAEPP and mCAEPP) for two-qutrit systems. It introduces a deterministic pre-processing scheme using mutually unbiased bases (MUBs) that overcomes convergence bottlenecks caused by marginal X-error probabilities, proving that MUB-adapted mCAEPP achieves unit asymptotic fidelity for any two-qutrit Pauli channel with initial fidelity > 1/3.
AI.motivation: Distilling high-dimensional quantum entanglement under realistic, general asymmetric noise remains a formidable challenge. Standard entanglement purification protocols fail under severe asymmetric noise.
AI.method: The paper investigates carrier-assisted entanglement purification protocols (CAEPP and mCAEPP) for two-qutrit systems, and introduces a deterministic pre-processing scheme based on mutually unbiased bases (MUBs) that rotates the qutrit phase space to establish primary-axis error dominance.
AI.result: Without adaptive pre-processing, convergence is strictly bottlenecked by marginal X-error probabilities. The MUB-adapted mCAEPP deterministically yields unit asymptotic fidelity for any two-qutrit Pauli channel with initial fidelity p00 > 1/3.
AI.conclusion: The MUB-based pre-processing successfully overcomes the convergence limitations imposed by asymmetric noise, achieving deterministic entanglement purification for two-qutrit systems under realistic conditions.

title: Ergotropy and Work Extraction in Quantum Heat Engines via Quantum Channels
summary: This paper explores quantum heat engines based on qubit and qutrit working media interacting with thermal environments through generalized amplitude damping (GAD) channels. We investigate how quantum channels can be employed to model heat absorption, dissipation, and work extraction in open quantum thermal machines, and derive the conditions required for positive work extraction. The effects of quantum correlations, emission probability, population redistribution, and system--environment interactions on the thermodynamic performance of the engine are systematically analyzed across different operational regimes. In addition, we examine the ergotropy of qubit and qutrit systems under dissipative dynamics to understand how environmental effects influence the maximum extractable work. Our results demonstrate that multilevel quantum systems exhibit enhanced work extraction capability and improved robustness against decoherence compared to two-level systems, providing further insight into the role of dissipative dynamics and quantum resources in realistic quantum thermodynamic devices.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates quantum heat engines using qubit and qutrit working media coupled to thermal environments via generalized amplitude damping channels, analyzing work extraction, quantum correlations, and ergotropy under dissipative dynamics.
AI.motivation: To understand how quantum channels can model heat absorption, dissipation, and work extraction in open quantum thermal machines, and to explore the advantages of multilevel quantum systems over two-level systems in realistic thermodynamic devices.
AI.method: Qubit and qutrit working media interacting with thermal environments through generalized amplitude damping (GAD) channels; systematic analysis of quantum correlations, emission probability, population redistribution, and system-environment interactions across different operational regimes.
AI.result: Multilevel quantum systems (qutrits) exhibit enhanced work extraction capability and improved robustness against decoherence compared to two-level systems (qubits).
AI.conclusion: Quantum channels provide a viable framework for modeling open quantum thermal machines, and higher-dimensional systems offer practical advantages for quantum thermodynamic devices under dissipative dynamics.

title: Photon Efficiency of High-Dimensional Quantum Key Distribution
summary: We investigate entanglement-based quantum key distribution protocols, with particular emphasis on their efficiency under realistic conditions of satellite quantum communications, where performance is limited by the low power of a received signal and background radiation. We focus on scenarios where each photon pair is used to encode multiple qubits in order to optimally utilize the weak signal. By optimizing over the source intensity and the number of encoded qubits we study the theoretical information limit for the QKD efficiency. We show that the optimal efficiency is attained for finite entangled photons pair production probability which is in contrast to conventional communication efficiency maximized in the limit of vanishing signal strength. The multiqubit encoding can enhance the secret key rate by up to an order of magnitude compared to single-qubit schemes.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates entanglement-based QKD protocols for satellite quantum communications, showing that optimal efficiency is achieved with finite entangled photon pair production probability (not vanishing signal strength) and that multi-qubit encoding can boost secret key rates by up to 10x compared to single-qubit schemes.
AI.motivation: To improve QKD efficiency under realistic satellite communication conditions where low signal power and background radiation severely limit performance, and to find optimal strategies for utilizing weak quantum signals.
AI.method: The authors analyze entanglement-based QKD protocols with multi-qubit encoding per photon pair, optimizing over source intensity and number of encoded qubits to study theoretical information limits for QKD efficiency.
AI.result: Optimal efficiency occurs at finite entangled photon pair production probability (contrary to conventional communication where efficiency is maximized at vanishing signal strength). Multi-qubit encoding enhances secret key rate by up to an order of magnitude over single-qubit schemes.
AI.conclusion: Multi-qubit encoding in entanglement-based QKD is a viable strategy for significantly improving performance in satellite quantum communications, and the optimal operating point involves finite source intensity rather than arbitrarily weak signals.

title: Impurity-induced loss bursts from anomalous scale-free localization in a non-Hermitian dissipative lattice
summary: We identify anomalous scale-free localization and the associated impurity-induced loss bursts in a non-Hermitian dissipative cross-stitch lattice. By a local basis rotation, the model is mapped onto an effective non-Hermitian Su-Schrieffer-Heeger lattice, where local impurities act as tunable effective boundaries. For the parameter choice considered here, tuning the impurity strength $η$ connects two effective open-boundary-condition-like limits, reached for $η\to0$ and $η\to\infty$, through generalized-boundary-condition regimes and the impurity-free periodic-boundary-condition point at $η=1$. For finite $η\notin\{0,1\}$, the spectral loops remain separated from the real-energy axis, while the eigenstates exhibit scale-free localization pinned by the impurity. Unlike conventional impurity-induced scale-free localization, the Lyapunov exponent depends explicitly on the eigenenergy, making the localization strength eigenstate dependent. We further show that this anomalous eigenmode structure produces an impurity-induced loss burst: the long-time integrated dissipation probability is strongly enhanced near an impurity-generated effective boundary even when the initial wave packet is far away. In the single-impurity case, the burst region consists of the impurity site and its adjacent effective-boundary site, and the effect occurs without imaginary-gap closing. For multiple impurities, local burst regions emerge around all impurities, while the dominant burst boundary is selected by the initial wave-packet position and the nonreciprocal drift direction. These results connect anomalous scale-free localization with controllable dissipation dynamics in non-Hermitian lattices.

AI.tldr: This paper discovers anomalous scale-free localization and impurity-induced loss bursts in a non-Hermitian cross-stitch lattice, where impurities act as tunable effective boundaries leading to eigenstate-dependent localization and enhanced dissipation near impurity-generated boundaries.
AI.motivation: To understand how local impurities in non-Hermitian lattices produce anomalous scale-free localization and controllable dissipation dynamics beyond conventional impurity effects.
AI.method: The model is mapped onto an effective non-Hermitian Su-Schrieffer-Heeger lattice via local basis rotation, where impurities act as tunable effective boundaries. Analytical and numerical analysis of spectral properties, Lyapunov exponents, and long-time integrated dissipation probability is performed.
AI.result: For finite η∉{0,1}, spectral loops stay separated from real-energy axis. Eigenstates show impurity-pinned scale-free localization with eigenenergy-dependent Lyapunov exponent. Impurity-induced loss bursts occur with enhanced dissipation near effective boundaries without imaginary-gap closing. For multiple impurities, local burst regions emerge around all impurities with the dominant one selected by initial wave-packet position and nonreciprocal drift.
AI.conclusion: The work connects anomalous scale-free localization with controllable dissipation dynamics in non-Hermitian lattices, revealing a new mechanism for manipulating wave-packet dynamics via impurity-tuned effective boundaries.

title: Quantum theory of a three-photon Kerr parametric oscillator
summary: We investigate the quantum properties of a nonlinear Kerr oscillator driven by a three-photon pump. We derive both exact and approximate analytical expressions for the ground state of this interacting model. The exact solution arises at an exact spectral degeneracy, while the approximate solution describes regimes of quasi-degeneracy of the energy spectrum. In both cases, the threefold (quasi)degenerate ground-state manifold consists of quantum superpositions of three macroscopically distinct states. These states differ qualitatively from conventional three-component Schrödinger's cat states due to the presence of squeezing with a distinctive parametric dependence. By varying the detuning between the oscillator and the three-photon pump, we show that the squeezing can be enhanced, suppressed, or even reversed, leading to a squeezing-to-anti-squeezing transition. We analyze the generation and stabilization of these superposition states, their robustness against perturbations and analytically quantify the leakage to excited states. Our analysis elucidates how the three-photon Kerr parametric oscillator can be used to encode a Kerr-cat qutrit protected against phase-flip errors.

AI.tldr: A three-photon driven Kerr oscillator exhibits a threefold degenerate ground state composed of squeezed Schrödinger cat-like states, with controllable squeezing that can transition to anti-squeezing, enabling a protected Kerr-cat qutrit for quantum information.
AI.motivation: To understand the quantum properties of a nonlinear Kerr oscillator under three-photon driving, particularly its ground-state structure and potential for encoding error-protected qutrits.
AI.method: Derivation of exact analytical solutions at spectral degeneracy and approximate solutions near degeneracy, analytical quantification of squeezing properties, perturbation analysis, and leakage characterization.
AI.result: The threefold degenerate manifold consists of squeezed three-component cat states with tunable squeezing; a squeezing-to-anti-squeezing transition occurs as detuning is varied; the system can encode a Kerr-cat qutrit protected against phase-flip errors.
AI.conclusion: The three-photon Kerr parametric oscillator provides a viable platform for realizing a protected qutrit with enhanced error resilience through controlled squeezing dynamics.

title: Towards transistor-based quantum computing
summary: In this work, we propose and study in depth a universal quantum computing architecture based on a quantum construction of transistors. Our teleportation-based quantum transistors, called ``telesistors'', are ground states of systems with symmetry-protected topological order, hence suppress certain noises and provide high-fidelity Clifford gates without the need for active error correction. This physical protection, quantified by the string order parameters, serves as a low-overhead foundation upon which conventional fault-tolerant encoding (e.g., with stabilizer codes) can be built to achieve universal quantum computation. This architecture shows rich connections with current known architectures, and some desirable merits especially compared with the qubit-based circuits regarding modularity, integration, and program storage. Our study shows that it is plausible to realize it with current technology in the near future.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a universal quantum computing architecture based on "telesistors" — teleportation-based quantum transistors that are ground states of symmetry-protected topological (SPT) ordered systems. These provide physical protection (quantified by string order parameters), enabling high-fidelity Clifford gates without active error correction, and can be combined with conventional fault-tolerant codes for universal computation. The architecture offers advantages in modularity, integration, and program storage over qubit-based circuits, and is plausible for near-term realization.
AI.motivation: To design a universal quantum computing architecture that achieves low-overhead noise suppression and high-fidelity Clifford gates without active error correction, while offering improved modularity, integration, and program storage compared to standard qubit-based circuits.
AI.method: The authors construct teleportation-based quantum transistors ("telesistors") from ground states of systems with symmetry-protected topological order. Physical protection is achieved via string order parameters, providing a low-overhead platform. Universal quantum computation is then enabled by layering conventional fault-tolerant encoding (e.g., stabilizer codes) on top of this physically protected foundation.
AI.result: The architecture yields high-fidelity Clifford gates without active error correction, exhibits rich connections to existing quantum architectures, and demonstrates advantages in modularity, integration, and program storage. The approach is assessed as plausible for near-term realization with current technology.
AI.conclusion: The proposed telesistor-based architecture offers a promising pathway toward universal quantum computing by combining physical protection from SPT order with conventional fault-tolerant encoding, potentially reducing overhead and improving scalability compared to qubit-based approaches.

title: Optimization of Secret Key Rate for BB84 under Collective Rotation Noise
summary: Practical quantum key distribution (QKD) systems operate under noise, but security of most protocols have been analyzed under ideal noiseless scenarios. In this work, we investigated security performance of BB84 protocol under effect of collective rotation noise. Using theoretical quantum information frameworks, we analyzed key security parameters including quantum bit error rate (QBER), mutual information and secret key rate (SKR). Security of protocol is studied under various eavesdropping scenarios based on intercept and resend attacks. Our results show that collective rotation noise has a significant impact on the information shared between the two parties. Particularly, we extended prior treatments by suggesting a noise engineering strategy where we identified a non-zero noise range where information accessed by Eve is minimized while corresponding SKR degradation remains relatively small. This analysis provide insights into robustness of BB84 protocol under realistic noisy channels and may contribute towards development of more resilient QKD systems.

AI.tldr: This paper analyzes the security of the BB84 QKD protocol under collective rotation noise, showing that noise significantly impacts information sharing and identifying a specific noise range where Eve's information is minimized while maintaining a relatively small secret key rate degradation.
AI.motivation: Practical QKD systems operate under noise, but most security analyses assume ideal noiseless scenarios, creating a gap between theory and practice.
AI.method: Using theoretical quantum information frameworks, the authors analyze QBER, mutual information, and secret key rate under collective rotation noise with intercept-and-resend eavesdropping attacks. They employ a noise engineering strategy to identify optimal noise ranges.
AI.result: Collective rotation noise significantly affects information shared between parties. A non-zero noise range exists where Eve's accessed information is minimized while SKR degradation remains relatively small.
AI.conclusion: The analysis provides insights into BB84 protocol robustness under realistic noisy channels and may contribute to developing more resilient QKD systems.

title: PIQC: Scalable Distributed Quantum Computing via Photonic Integration of Designed Molecular Quantum Nodes
summary: There is a growing consensus that large-scale, fault-tolerant quantum computing (FTQC) necessitates high-fidelity photonic interconnects to overcome the scaling limits of monolithic architectures. However, most current platforms were not originally designed for native photonic connectivity and require significant engineering overhead. To overcome these fundamental hardware limitations, we recently introduced a rationally designed organic molecule that serves as an ideal quantum node, featuring a robust qubit-photon interface (QPI) and a long-lived nuclear-spin register. In this work, we present PIQC (Photonic Integrated Quantum Circuits), a distributed architecture designed to scale these molecular nodes into a functional quantum computer. The PIQC framework integrates five mutually reinforcing innovations: (i) Designer molecular qubits, i.e. carbene molecules in an isosteric host that provide millisecond-coherence electron spins with high spectral stability and spin-dependent optical emission, (ii) deterministic nuclear registers made of synthetically placed $^{13}$C or $^{14}$N labels that enable fast ($\sim 1~μ$s), high-fidelity electron-nuclear gates, (iii) hybrid photonic integration, which allows molecular films to seamlessly integrate with existing mature fabrication technologies, e.g. thin-film lithium niobate (TFLN), (iv) heralded entanglement protocols that can tolerate up to 70% photon loss, and (v) stairway Floquetification, i.e. high-rate quantum low-density parity-check (qLDPC) codes that are converted into Floquet codes, reducing syndrome extraction to weight-two Bell-pair measurements that match PIQC's networked hardware. PIQC offers a hardware-efficient, commercially viable pathway toward a utility-scale quantum computer based on distributed FTQC.

AI.tldr: PIQC proposes a distributed quantum computing architecture using designer organic molecular nodes (carbene molecules) with photonic interconnects, integrating five innovations: molecular qubits with millisecond coherence, deterministic nuclear registers, hybrid photonic integration (e.g., TFLN), heralded entanglement tolerant to 70% photon loss, and stairway Floquetification for qLDPC codes—aiming for utility-scale fault-tolerant quantum computing.
AI.motivation: Large-scale fault-tolerant quantum computing requires high-fidelity photonic interconnects to overcome scaling limits of monolithic architectures, but existing platforms lack native photonic connectivity and incur significant engineering overhead.
AI.method: PIQC integrates five components: (1) designer carbene molecular qubits with millisecond-coherence electron spins and spin-dependent optical emission in isosteric hosts; (2) deterministic nuclear registers via synthetically placed ¹³C/¹⁴N labels enabling fast (~1 μs) high-fidelity electron-nuclear gates; (3) hybrid photonic integration with mature platforms like thin-film lithium niobate; (4) heralded entanglement protocols tolerating up to 70% photon loss; (5) stairway Floquetification converting high-rate qLDPC codes into Floquet codes for weight-two Bell-pair measurements.
AI.result: A hardware-efficient, commercially viable distributed architecture toward utility-scale FTQC, with molecular nodes providing robust qubit-photon interfaces and long-lived nuclear-spin registers.
AI.conclusion: PIQC offers a practical pathway to scale molecular quantum nodes into a functional, distributed fault-tolerant quantum computer using rationally designed organic molecules and photonic integration.

title: Velocity-Controlled Directional Readout of Single Photons
summary: Photodetection is usually treated in the frame in which the detector is at rest relative to the optical apparatus. We show that uniform motion of an electric Glauber detector changes the single-click POVM realized on two counterpropagating single-photon modes. Motion Doppler-shifts the alternatives in the detector frame; finite bandwidth then converts propagation direction into a detection bias without decohering the photon. For a Lorentzian response near one Doppler branch, the readout crosses from phase-sensitive to direction-sensitive with a quality-factor-enhanced onset. Finite-time integration adds Doppler-beat visibility loss, separating passive covariance from measurement change.

AI.tldr: Uniform motion of a Glauber detector changes the POVM on counterpropagating single-photon modes via Doppler shifts and finite bandwidth, creating a direction-sensitive detection bias without decoherence, with a quality-factor-enhanced transition from phase-sensitive to direction-sensitive readout.
AI.motivation: To challenge the conventional assumption that detectors are at rest relative to the optical apparatus, and to explore how uniform motion affects single-photon detection measurements beyond standard Doppler effects.
AI.method: The authors consider an electric Glauber detector in uniform motion relative to the optical setup, analyzing the single-click POVM on two counterpropagating single-photon modes. They account for Doppler shifts, finite detector bandwidth, Lorentzian response near one Doppler branch, and finite-time integration effects.
AI.result: Motion Doppler-shifts detection alternatives, and finite bandwidth converts propagation direction into a detection bias without decoherence. For a Lorentzian response near one Doppler branch, the readout transitions from phase-sensitive to direction-sensitive with quality-factor-enhanced onset. Finite-time integration introduces Doppler-beat visibility loss, separating passive covariance from actual measurement change.
AI.conclusion: Detector motion fundamentally alters the measurement structure for single-photon modes, with the direction-sensitivity arising from Doppler-broadened detection—this is a genuine change in the measurement, not merely a passive coordinate transformation.

title: Enhanced Reinforcement Learning-based Process Synthesis via Quantum Computing
summary: In this work, we present quantum reinforcement learning (RL) as a solution strategy for process synthesis problems. Building on our prior work, we develop a generalized framework that formally poses process synthesis as a Markov decision process and introduces quantum-enhanced RL algorithms to solve it with improved scalability. Earlier implementations of quantum-based RL for process synthesis were limited by qubit requirements, which scaled poorly with problem complexity. This work overcomes this challenge by introducing state encoding algorithms to decouple qubit requirements from problem size. A classical RL-based solution strategy is used as a baseline to benchmark the quantum algorithms under identical training conditions. All algorithms are evaluated across a flowsheet synthesis problem of increasing unit counts to analyze their performance and scalability. Results show that all approaches are capable of identifying the optimal flowsheet designs in small design spaces. For moderate-scale unit counts, quantum approaches demonstrate competitive performance on a per-episode basis and improved efficiency on a per-parameter basis versus the classical RL benchmark. This work provides a foundation for future quantum computing applications within process systems engineering, establishes a controlled benchmark for comparing classical and quantum algorithms, and shows that the proposed quantum variants remain competitive for the process synthesis problem examined in this work.

AI.tldr: This paper presents quantum reinforcement learning (RL) for process synthesis, introducing state encoding algorithms to decouple qubit requirements from problem size, and shows quantum approaches remain competitive or more efficient than classical RL baselines across flowsheet synthesis problems.
AI.motivation: Prior quantum-based RL for process synthesis suffered from poor scalability due to qubit requirements that grew with problem complexity; this work aims to overcome that limitation and systematically benchmark quantum vs. classical RL for process synthesis.
AI.method: The authors formalize process synthesis as a Markov decision process, introduce state encoding algorithms to decouple qubit requirements from problem size, implement quantum-enhanced RL algorithms, and benchmark against classical RL under identical training conditions across flowsheet synthesis problems with increasing unit counts.
AI.result: All approaches identify optimal flowsheet designs in small spaces; at moderate-scale unit counts, quantum approaches show competitive per-episode performance and improved per-parameter efficiency compared to classical RL.
AI.conclusion: The work provides a foundation for quantum computing in process systems engineering, establishes a controlled benchmark for classical vs. quantum algorithms, and demonstrates that proposed quantum variants remain competitive for the examined process synthesis problem.

title: Enhanced quantum metrology by criticality-assisted noncommutative preparation
summary: Quantum criticality is a resource for quantum-enhanced metrology, but existing schemes face intrinsic limitations. These arise because using criticality directly in the encoding dynamics restricts the accessible parameters to those explicitly supported by the critical Hamiltonian, and the requirement for critical conditions narrows the effective estimation range. To solve this, we introduce a general framework termed criticality-assisted noncommutative preparation (CANP). In this approach, critical evolution is employed as a state-preparation resource. We establish the underlying algebraic conditions and show that the intrinsic noncommutativity between the preparation and encoding operations leads to a genuine enhancement of the quantum Fisher information (QFI). Remarkably, this enhancement may be achieved at fixed total sensing time and energy cost. The effect is quantified by the Wigner-Yanase skew information, which measures noncommutativity and exhibits the same critical scaling as the QFI. We demonstrate effective use of CANP in the quantum Rabi and Lipkin-Meshkov-Glick models. Our results establish CANP as a robust technique to effectively implement criticality-enhanced quantum metrology.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces criticality-assisted noncommutative preparation (CANP), a framework that uses quantum critical evolution as a state-preparation resource rather than as the encoding dynamics, overcoming limitations of existing criticality-enhanced metrology schemes. The key mechanism is noncommutativity between preparation and encoding operations, which yields genuine quantum Fisher information enhancement at fixed sensing time and energy cost, quantified by Wigner-Yanase skew information. The method is demonstrated in the quantum Rabi and Lipkin-Meshkov-Glick models.
AI.motivation: Existing criticality-enhanced quantum metrology schemes have intrinsic limitations: they restrict accessible parameters to those explicitly supported by the critical Hamiltonian, and the requirement for critical conditions narrows the effective estimation range. The authors seek to overcome these constraints.
AI.method: The authors propose criticality-assisted noncommutative preparation (CANP), where critical evolution is used as a state-preparation resource rather than as the encoding dynamics. They establish algebraic conditions based on noncommutativity between preparation and encoding operations to enhance the quantum Fisher information, quantified by Wigner-Yanase skew information.
AI.result: The intrinsic noncommutativity between preparation and encoding operations leads to genuine QFI enhancement, achievable at fixed total sensing time and energy cost. The Wigner-Yanase skew information exhibits the same critical scaling as the QFI. The method is demonstrated effectively in the quantum Rabi and Lipkin-Meshkov-Glick models.
AI.conclusion: CANP establishes a robust technique to effectively implement criticality-enhanced quantum metrology, overcoming the limitations of direct critical encoding approaches.

title: High-order harmonic generation from an atom in a disordered environment
summary: Using one-dimensional simulations analyzed through the lens of open quantum systems, we study the photoelectron's strong-field dynamics from an atom surrounded by a scattering environment stochastically structured. We theoretically investigate high-order harmonic generation from this situation. We show that local dephasing of the photoelectron wavepacket induced by elastic scattering leads to global decoherence. This drives a transition from quantum to classical behavior, as witnessed by the photoelectron probability density localizing around specific trajectories of the classical analog system: unstable periodic orbits. This phenomenon mirrors quantum scars traditionally observed in the eigenfunctions of time-independent systems, such as quantum billiards. Here, it emerges in-situ within a time-dependent framework, manifesting directly in the real-time dynamics from the ground state rather than solely through spectral analysis.

AI.tldr: The paper studies high-order harmonic generation in an atom surrounded by a stochastically structured scattering environment using one-dimensional simulations and open quantum systems theory. It finds that elastic scattering-induced dephasing causes quantum-to-classical transition, with photoelectron probability density localizing around classical unstable periodic orbits—a time-domain analogue of quantum scars.
AI.motivation: To understand how a stochastic scattering environment affects strong-field dynamics and high-order harmonic generation, particularly the transition from quantum to classical behavior induced by decoherence.
AI.method: One-dimensional simulations analyzed through the lens of open quantum systems theory, studying photoelectron strong-field dynamics in an atom with a stochastically structured scattering environment.
AI.result: Local dephasing of the photoelectron wavepacket due to elastic scattering induces global decoherence, driving a quantum-to-classical transition. The photoelectron probability density localizes around classical unstable periodic orbits—a time-domain manifestation of quantum scars emerging from real-time dynamics.
AI.conclusion: Quantum scar-like phenomena can emerge in-situ within time-dependent frameworks from the ground state, not just through spectral analysis of time-independent systems like quantum billiards.

title: Collapse of the state vector and nonlocal correlations in quantum mechanics
summary: It is shown how to obtain state vectors associated with measurements on the separated subystems of an entangled state, revealing how a single wavefunction encodes a set of statistical measurement outcomes. The result explains why measurements on the subsystems give definite outcomes and why measurements on one subsystem are correlated with those on the other. It is therefore concluded that the theory of quantum mechanics, without nonlinearities or \emph{ad hoc} assertions, can explain both the mechanism of state vector collapse and the reason for the paradoxical nonlocal correlations between separated subsystems.The theory also explains how quantum correlations, including correlations that violate Bell's inequality, are read out by classical measurements.

AI.tldr: This paper shows how state vectors associated with measurements on subsystems of an entangled state can be derived, explaining how a single wavefunction encodes statistical measurement outcomes, why subsystem measurements yield definite results, and why correlations exist between separated subsystems—concluding that quantum mechanics itself, without nonlinearities or ad hoc assertions, explains state vector collapse and nonlocal correlations, including those violating Bell's inequality.
AI.motivation: To resolve the measurement problem and the paradox of nonlocal correlations in quantum mechanics without resorting to nonlinear modifications or ad hoc collapse postulates.
AI.method: Analytical derivation showing how state vectors associated with measurements on separated subsystems of an entangled state are obtained from the wavefunction.
AI.result: The wavefunction inherently encodes a set of statistical measurement outcomes; measurements on subsystems yield definite outcomes; correlations between separated subsystems emerge naturally without additional postulates.
AI.conclusion: Standard quantum mechanics (without nonlinearities or ad hoc assertions) can explain both wavefunction collapse and nonlocal quantum correlations, including Bell inequality violations, as read out by classical measurements.

title: Boundary Geometry Turns Entanglement into Steering
summary: Entanglement does not in general imply Einstein-Podolsky-Rosen steering. We identify a boundary-geometric mechanism that closes this gap on product-null boundary strata of two-qubit state space, where Bob's conditional states touch the boundary of the Bloch ball. The key obstruction is local: if a projective assemblage approaches a Bloch-sphere boundary contact with a first-order tangential displacement but only a second-order inward defect, then no finite-measure local-hidden-state model can reproduce it. For two-qubit states with a product vector in the kernel, this boundary contact is exactly the tangency of Bob's steering ellipsoid to the Bloch sphere. At such a product-null tangency, a single tangential coherence controls both partial-transpose negativity and the boundary-contact scaling obstruction. The same boundary minor gives a compact experimental witness: once the product-null contact is verified or guaranteed, the tangential coherence supplies the steering signal. Consequently, every entangled two-qubit rank-two state, and every entangled rank-three state whose null space is spanned by a product vector, is two-way projectively steerable. The same boundary idea extends to arbitrary steering cuts: the Bloch-sphere contact is replaced by a rank-deficient trusted conditional state, and support-kernel first-order coherence implies both NPT entanglement and projective steering.

AI.tldr: The paper identifies a boundary-geometric mechanism explaining why entanglement does not always imply Einstein-Podolsky-Rosen (EPR) steering, showing that when Bob's conditional states touch the Bloch ball boundary with specific tangential coherence conditions, projective steering emerges. This resolves the gap between entanglement and steering for certain two-qubit states, particularly rank-two and specific rank-three states, and provides experimental witnesses.
AI.motivation: To resolve the known gap where entanglement does not generally imply EPR steering by identifying the geometric and algebraic conditions under which this gap closes.
AI.method: Analysis of product-null boundary strata of two-qubit state space; examination of projective assemblages approaching Bloch-sphere boundary contact with first-order tangential displacement and second-order inward defect; study of steering ellipsoid tangency and tangential coherence; extension to arbitrary steering cuts via rank-deficient trusted conditional states.
AI.result: Every entangled two-qubit rank-two state, and every entangled rank-three state whose null space is spanned by a product vector, is two-way projectively steerable. The tangential coherence simultaneously controls partial-transpose negativity and the boundary-contact scaling obstruction, providing a compact experimental witness.
AI.conclusion: The boundary-geometric mechanism closes the entanglement-steering gap for specific state classes, and the same boundary idea generalizes to arbitrary steering cuts where support-kernel first-order coherence implies both NPT entanglement and projective steering.

title: Semidefinite Programming for Optimal Quantum Cloning: A Computational Framework
summary: While algebraic derivations establish theoretical limits for quantum cloning, practical implementations require explicit operator representations that are often unavailable analytically. We present a computational framework that reformulates cloning optimization as a search over completely positive trace-preserving maps using the Choi-Jamiolkowski isomorphism and Semidefinite Programming. The framework (i) numerically certifies global optimality through primal-dual strong duality and (ii) automatically extracts operational Kraus operators from the optimal Choi matrix via spectral decomposition. We systematically treat universal, phase-covariant, asymmetric, and entanglement cloning scenarios, providing -for the first time - a unified computational catalogue of explicit, implementable Kraus representations across all major cloning families, including higher-order processes and arbitrary input state distributions. As an application, we analyse optimal cloning attacks on BB84 under depolarizing noise, demonstrating how the extracted operators enable quantitative security analysis in realistic noisy quantum channels. An open-source implementation enables community validation and extension.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a computational framework using Semidefinite Programming and the Choi-Jamiolkowski isomorphism to numerically derive optimal, physically implementable Kraus operators for quantum cloning across all major cloning families, with application to security analysis of BB84 under noise.
AI.motivation: While algebraic derivations provide theoretical limits for quantum cloning, practical implementations require explicit operator representations that are often unavailable analytically.
AI.method: The framework reformulates cloning optimization as a search over CPTP maps using the Choi-Jamiolkowski isomorphism and Semidefinite Programming, with global optimality certified via primal-dual strong duality and Kraus operators extracted from the optimal Choi matrix via spectral decomposition.
AI.result: Provides the first unified computational catalogue of explicit, implementable Kraus representations across universal, phase-covariant, asymmetric, and entanglement cloning scenarios, including higher-order processes and arbitrary input state distributions.
AI.conclusion: The extracted operators enable quantitative security analysis of optimal cloning attacks on BB84 under depolarizing noise in realistic noisy quantum channels. An open-source implementation supports community validation.

title: Benchmarking a machine-learning differential equations solver on a neutral-atom logical processor
comment: PM, EG, AL and EP contributed equally
summary: We report on a performance comparison between physical and logical computations on a prototypical machine-learning application: solving differential equations using quantum kernel methods. The algorithm is implemented on an atom-based logical quantum processor, both at the physical and logical levels. We show that the kernel estimated from the logical implementation performs better than its physical counterpart on relevant metrics. We observe how such performance improvement can be traced back to specific noise-induced errors detected by the chosen encoding. We apply the computed quantum kernel to the task of solving differential equations, confirming how the superior performance of a logical quantum kernel is retained also at an end-to-end applicative level. Our findings show that experimental validation of end-to-end protocols can already highlight the positive impact of fault-tolerant implementations despite their higher quantum resource count, and guide application-informed architectural choices.

AI.tldr: This paper compares physical vs. logical quantum computations on a machine-learning application (solving differential equations using quantum kernel methods) implemented on an atom-based logical quantum processor. The logical kernel outperforms the physical one, with improvements traceable to noise-induced errors detected by the encoding. The advantage persists at the end-to-end applicative level, showing that fault-tolerant implementations can already demonstrate positive impact despite higher resource requirements.
AI.motivation: To experimentally compare physical and logical quantum computations on a practical machine-learning task (solving differential equations via quantum kernel methods) and assess whether fault-tolerant implementations can provide tangible benefits despite their higher quantum resource overhead.
AI.method: Implemented a quantum kernel method for solving differential equations on an atom-based logical quantum processor at both physical and logical levels. Compared kernel estimation performance and end-to-end applicative results, tracing performance differences to noise-induced errors detected by the chosen encoding.
AI.result: The logical quantum kernel outperformed the physical counterpart on relevant metrics; the performance improvement was traced to specific noise-induced errors detected by encoding; the superior performance of the logical quantum kernel persisted at the end-to-end applicative level for solving differential equations.
AI.conclusion: Experimental validation of end-to-end protocols can already demonstrate the positive impact of fault-tolerant implementations despite higher quantum resource counts, and can guide application-informed architectural choices.

title: Software Between Quantum and Machine Learning -- And Down to Pulses
summary:
Contemporary quantum computing platforms remain, in essence, programmable physical systems whose control is typically mediated through unitary gate abstractions. While such abstractions provide a uniform interface, they obscure important aspects of the underlying hardware and may limit the exploitation of its full capabilities. Direct operation at the control-pulse level offers a more expressive and physically faithful paradigm, enabling, for instance, the implementation of tailored error-mitigation and optimisation strategies. However, this increased expressivity comes at the cost of greater quantum software development complexity, necessitating structured and accessible tooling.
  We present a software framework, integrated within the QML-Essentials package, that extends quantum machine learning (QML) methodologies to encompass pulse-level modelling. By embedding quantum optimal control techniques within a QML setting, our approach enables the seamless combination of gate-based and pulse-level representations. The framework provides a comprehensive suite of modelling and analytical capabilities. In particular, we introduce composable ansatz constructions based on interchangeable building blocks, and support for end-to-end optimisation of pulse parameters. Motivated by the central role of quantum Fourier models, we further incorporate a range of Fourier-analytic diagnostics, complemented by extended measures of entanglement. All performance-critical components are implemented in a high-performance environment using JAX and supported by a dedicated quantum simulator. Taken together, the framework facilitates reproducible and systematic investigations, while bridging the conceptual and practical divide between abstract circuit models and hardware-aware optimisation. It provides a robust foundation for future developments at the intersection of QML and quantum control.

AI.tldr: A software framework integrated within QML-Essentials that extends quantum machine learning to pulse-level control, bridging gate-based abstractions and hardware-aware optimization via quantum optimal control techniques, composable ansatz constructions, Fourier-analytic diagnostics, and JAX-based high-performance simulation.
AI.motivation: Gate-based abstractions obscure important hardware details and limit exploitation of full quantum computing capabilities; direct pulse-level control offers more expressivity but increases software complexity, necessitating structured tooling.
AI.method: Embedding quantum optimal control techniques within a QML setting to combine gate-based and pulse-level representations; composable ansatz constructions from interchangeable building blocks; end-to-end optimization of pulse parameters; Fourier-analytic diagnostics and extended entanglement measures; all implemented in JAX with a dedicated quantum simulator.
AI.result: A comprehensive framework providing seamless integration of gate-based and pulse-level paradigms, reproducible systematic investigations, and bridging abstract circuit models with hardware-aware optimization.
AI.conclusion: The framework provides a robust foundation for future developments at the intersection of quantum machine learning and quantum control, enabling tailored error-mitigation and optimization strategies.

title: Quantum Nonlocality and Device-Independent Randomness are Robust to Noisy Signaling Channels
summary: Given a pair of isolated devices that accept random binary inputs and return binary outputs, a user can deduce from the observed data alone if the underlying mechanism can be explained classically. Bell's theorem further states that a classical explanation can be ruled out if the devices perform certain measurements on an entangled quantum state, underpinning the security of cryptographic protocols that are device-independent (DI). For certain protocols, such as those performed in a tight space, it might be difficult to perfectly enforce the non-signaling assumption required in Bell's theorem. This prompts the question: is quantum nonlocality robust to such imperfections? We show that if a binary channel sends a noisy copy of one party's input to the other before any measurements take place, the answer is yes. We completely characterize the vertices and facets of the local polytope in this scenario, and identify Bell inequalities that certify non-signaling quantum correlations. This is possible even when a near perfect copy of the input is sent. We go on to show that the identified inequalities are more robust to depolarizing noise than the Clauser-Horne-Shimony-Holt inequality when certifying DI randomness in this scenario. In addition, we characterize the local polytope when both parties receive a noisy copy of each other's input and make similar conclusions, leaving many new potential Bell inequalities to be explored.

AI.tldr: This paper shows that quantum nonlocality can be certified even when a noisy copy of one party's input is leaked to the other before measurements, violating the strict non-signaling assumption required in standard Bell tests. The authors characterize the local polytope's vertices and facets, identify robust Bell inequalities, and demonstrate improved performance over CHSH for device-independent randomness certification under depolarizing noise.
AI.motivation: To determine whether quantum nonlocality (and thus device-independent protocols) remains valid when the strict non-signaling assumption is relaxed, e.g., due to tight physical constraints that make perfect isolation difficult.
AI.method: The authors completely characterize the vertices and facets of the local polytope under a noisy pre-measurement communication channel, identify new Bell inequalities, and analyze their robustness to depolarizing noise for certifying DI randomness.
AI.result: Quantum nonlocality is robust even when a near-perfect noisy copy of one party's input is sent to the other. The identified Bell inequalities are more robust to depolarizing noise than CHSH for DI randomness certification. Similar conclusions hold when both parties receive noisy copies of each other's inputs.
AI.conclusion: The strict non-signaling assumption can be relaxed while still certifying nonlocal quantum correlations, with the identified inequalities offering advantages over CHSH for DI randomness in imperfect isolation scenarios.

title: Evidence of Quantum Machine Learning Advantage with Tens of Noisy Qubits
summary: Learning problems involving quantum data are natural candidates for demonstrating an advantage in quantum machine learning. Recent results indicate that, for certain tasks and under noiseless conditions, coherent processing of quantum data outperforms fixed-measurement schemes followed by classical processing. It remained uncertain whether this performance gap persists at a finite scale, and in the presence of noise that is unavoidable with current quantum devices. In this work, we present simulations and analysis of the performance of existing hardware on a learning problem known to exhibit asymptotic advantage, now subjected to noisy quantum data. Comparing coherent quantum processing directly against fixed-measurement schemes, our results demonstrate a clear performance separation at a scale of just 30 to 40 noisy qubits. Already at this scale, the fundamental bottleneck is no longer classical computation but data acquisition; matching the noisy coherent protocol with measure-first strategies would still require months or even years of measurements. By systematically evaluating hardware constraints such as state preparation, gate errors, readout errors, connectivity, and coherence times, we provide evidence that a demonstration of such a strong learning advantage is accessible on near-term devices.

AI.tldr: At a scale of 30–40 noisy qubits, coherent quantum processing of quantum data outperforms fixed-measurement classical schemes by such a large margin that the bottleneck shifts from computation to data acquisition; matching performance with classical strategies would require months or years of measurements.
AI.motivation: To determine whether the asymptotic quantum advantage for learning from quantum data persists at finite scales and under realistic noise conditions present in current quantum devices.
AI.method: Simulations and analysis comparing coherent quantum processing against fixed-measurement schemes on a learning problem with known asymptotic advantage, subjecting both to noisy quantum data and evaluating hardware constraints (state preparation, gate/readout errors, connectivity, coherence times).
AI.result: A clear performance separation appears at just 30–40 noisy qubits; the bottleneck becomes data acquisition (months/years of measurements for measure-first strategies) rather than classical computation.
AI.conclusion: A demonstration of strong quantum learning advantage is accessible on near-term devices, contingent on systematically evaluated hardware constraints.

title: Modeling and Resource Optimization for Quantum Oracles
summary: Quantum computing has demonstrated its significant advantage over supercomputing for specific applications and shown promising prospect, such as machine learning, cryptography, finance, etc.. Quantum oracles are very common in many quantum algorithms and oracle resource consumption directly affects algorithm performance. However, existing oracle designs often exhibit high resource overhead and limited compatibility. Moreover, structured description tools and complexity analysis methods are lacked. In this work, we introduces a Hierarchical Recursive Synthesis-Evaluation (HRSE) model, enabling formal description and precise quantum gate complexity analysis of oracles. Based on this model, we propose an Adaptive Space-depth Trade-off (ASDT) algorithm for generating oracle structures under a fixed qubit constraint. We provide a theoretical proof showing that the ASDT algorithm achieves the optimal gate count for a given number of qubits. Experimental results show that the ASDT algorithm reduces the average quantum circuit depth by 53.99% compared with the W-cycle approach, with the number of variables being 10, 15, and 20, respectively.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a Hierarchical Recursive Synthesis-Evaluation (HRSE) model for formal description and complexity analysis of quantum oracles, and proposes an Adaptive Space-depth Trade-off (ASDT) algorithm that achieves optimal gate count under fixed qubit constraints, reducing average circuit depth by 53.99% compared to the W-cycle approach.
AI.motivation: Existing quantum oracle designs suffer from high resource overhead, limited compatibility, and a lack of structured description tools and complexity analysis methods, motivating the need for a formal model and optimization algorithm.
AI.method: The authors propose the HRSE model for formal description and gate complexity analysis of oracles, and the ASDT algorithm for generating oracle structures optimized under fixed qubit constraints, with theoretical proof of optimal gate count.
AI.result: The ASDT algorithm reduces average quantum circuit depth by 53.99% compared to the W-cycle approach for variable counts of 10, 15, and 20.
AI.conclusion: The HRSE model and ASDT algorithm provide a formal framework and practical optimization for quantum oracle design, significantly improving resource efficiency and enabling better scalability for quantum algorithms.

title: Combining non-parametric quantum states and MERA tensor networks for ground-state optimization
summary: Hybrid tensor networks offer a promising route to enhance the expressivity of classical tensor network methods by incorporating quantum states prepared on a quantum computer. Existing approaches are limited by the variational optimization of the quantum component of the tensor network. In this work, we introduce an alternative strategy that combines a non-parametric quantum state prepared through quantum annealing and a classical isometric tensor network. The latter is variationally optimized while the former is used as a fixed, boundary tensor resource in the form of classical shadows. We demonstrate the feasibility of this approach through extensive numerical simulations on the transverse-field Ising model, showing that the optimization procedure remains robust under statistical and hardware noise. Moreover, our results indicate that our newly proposed setup improves the accuracy of the obtained ground state approximation compared to the original quantum simulation, without increasing the depth of the applied quantum circuits. Therefore, this setup offers a practical route to scale variational quantum algorithms towards the quantum utility scale.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a hybrid quantum-classical tensor network approach where a non-parametric quantum state prepared via quantum annealing is used as a fixed boundary tensor (via classical shadows) combined with a variationally optimized classical isometric tensor network, demonstrating improved ground state accuracy on the transverse-field Ising model without increasing quantum circuit depth.
AI.motivation: Existing hybrid tensor network methods are limited by the variational optimization of the quantum component; the authors aim to overcome this by using a non-parametric, fixed quantum state from quantum annealing, avoiding costly quantum variational loops.
AI.method: Combines a non-parametric quantum state prepared through quantum annealing (used as a fixed boundary tensor via classical shadows) with a classical isometric tensor network that is variationally optimized, tested on the transverse-field Ising model with noise simulations.
AI.result: The optimization procedure remains robust under statistical and hardware noise, and the hybrid setup improves ground state approximation accuracy compared to the original quantum simulation without increasing quantum circuit depth.
AI.conclusion: This hybrid setup offers a practical route to scale variational quantum algorithms toward quantum utility scale by avoiding deep quantum circuits and costly variational optimization of the quantum component.

title: An Exponential Sample-Complexity Advantage for Coherent Quantum Inference
summary: Standard quantum inference converts quantum data into classical outputs. We study an alternative inference setting in which the desired output is quantum, preserving coherence. Such settings include quantum purity amplification (QPA), mixed-state approximate purification or cloning, and density matrix exponentiation. We show that such protocols can achieve exponentially lower sample complexity than incoherent, measurement-mediated protocols. For QPA with principal eigenstate targets and $d$-dimensional inputs, coherent processing achieves error $\varepsilon$ using $O(1/\varepsilon)$ copies, versus the $Ω(d/\varepsilon)$ copies required by any incoherent protocol. Together, these sharp coherent-incoherent separations seed a theory of coherent quantum inference, with an entanglement-breaking limit identifying the optimal incoherent counterpart of each coherent protocol.

AI.tldr: Coherent quantum inference, where outputs are quantum states preserving coherence, achieves exponentially lower sample complexity than incoherent measurement-mediated protocols. For quantum purity amplification, coherent processing needs only O(1/ε) copies versus Ω(d/ε) for incoherent methods, establishing a fundamental separation and a theory of coherent quantum inference with an entanglement-breaking limit.
AI.motivation: To study quantum inference settings where the desired output is quantum (coherent) rather than classical, and to demonstrate that such coherent protocols can achieve fundamentally lower sample complexity than incoherent, measurement-mediated approaches.
AI.method: The paper studies coherent quantum inference protocols including quantum purity amplification (QPA), mixed-state approximate purification/cloning, and density matrix exponentiation. It establishes a theoretical framework using an entanglement-breaking limit to identify optimal incoherent counterparts of coherent protocols, and analyzes sample complexity separations between coherent and incoherent approaches.
AI.result: Coherent processing for QPA with principal eigenstate targets and d-dimensional inputs achieves error ε using O(1/ε) copies, while incoherent protocols require Ω(d/ε) copies—a sharp exponential separation. Similar separations hold for other coherent inference tasks.
AI.conclusion: These sharp coherent-incoherent separations establish a theory of coherent quantum inference, where the entanglement-breaking limit identifies the optimal incoherent counterpart for each coherent protocol, revealing fundamental advantages of preserving coherence in quantum inference.
